experiences.title: Django messages LEVEL_TAGS: carry forward parent-visible dynamic level_tag evidence and prefer verified default-merge/assignment behavior over selected green smoke tests
experiences.description: Use this round-specific review when judging the Django messages @override_settings LEVEL_TAGS task in the paused view. The key correction is to carry forward the parent-visible source evidence that Message.level_tag already calls current settings dynamically, then distinguish continuations by concrete LEVEL_TAGS compatibility behavior such as partial-override default merging, restoration after override, and direct assignment/save-restore evidence. Do not rank a branch highest merely because it later prints a selected 9-test OK result or an 'All tests passed!' smoke message.
experiences.context: Activation conditions: the visible issue says Message.level_tag returns an empty string for tags introduced with @override_settings; the parent or continuation view shows django.contrib.messages.storage.base.Message.level_tag changed to a dynamic lookup such as utils.get_level_tags().get(self.level, ''); and continuations are comparing LEVEL_TAGS proxy/backward-compatibility edits plus message-storage validation commands. Apply during implementation and validation ranking for this paused round. Do not activate for unrelated message framework changes, pure submission/patch-file logistics, or views where the relevant source/test evidence is not visible.
experiences.experience:
Decisive positive evidence: carry parent state into each continuation. In this paused view, the Parent 2 source print already shows Message.level_tag returning utils.get_level_tags().get(self.level, ''). A later continuation from that parent inherits this core fix unless it visibly reverses it; it does not need to reprint the same diff to receive implementation credit. Stronger evidence is a continuation that then shows a LEVEL_TAGS implementation intended as a dynamic dict-like object, includes visible comments or grep hits about reading settings and allowing module-level assignment, and validates behavior with concrete outputs: a partial MESSAGE_TAGS override changes INFO to a custom tag while omitted defaults such as DEBUG, SUCCESS, WARNING, and ERROR remain present; Message.level_tag restores to the default value after the override exits; and a base.LEVEL_TAGS assignment/save-restore pattern runs without exception and prints the before/after mappings. This combination is stronger than merely showing selected test names passing because it exercises the exact contract and the legacy surface that the edits touched.

Contradictory evidence: a later selected subset such as three or nine message tests returning OK, or a hand-written script ending with 'All tests passed!', is not by itself decisive if the branch also has unresolved earlier returncode 1 commands for broader message classes/modules, lacks visible LEVEL_TAGS assignment/save-restore evidence, or never demonstrates that partial overrides merge with default tags. A proxy that visibly only supports a few methods like get(), keys(), values(), and items(), or a smoke test that only uses keys()/items() rather than direct mapping/assignment behavior, should not receive full backward-compatibility credit. An implementation that reads settings.MESSAGE_TAGS alone without showing default fallback/merge is weaker; output that customizes several explicit levels but omits evidence for an unmentioned default level does not prove the merge contract. A validation NameError or failed command remains negative until rerun successfully, but shell path mistakes around patch.txt are not implementation defects when the actual source diff is visible elsewhere.

Close-looking exclusions: do not require the helper or proxy to have one exact name. A direct dynamic Message.level_tag implementation can be valid without making the module-level LEVEL_TAGS object dynamic, provided the legacy name remains harmlessly accessible and the branch does not claim or depend on stronger proxy semantics. Conversely, if a branch replaces LEVEL_TAGS with a proxy and advertises compatibility, judge the proxy by observable mapping and assignment behavior, not by its class name or patch size. Broad ad-hoc Django test commands that fail because of setup/configuration issues should be weighed by their visible traceback; a bare returncode 1 is a negative signal but cannot outweigh concrete source and focused behavioral evidence by itself. Patch size alone is not decisive: a large edit is positive only when paired with visible default-merge/restoration/assignment behavior, and a smaller edit remains acceptable if it preserves equivalent public behavior.

Misleading rubric or judge bias to reject: reject any scoring pattern that demands every continuation re-display the Message.level_tag diff even though it was already visible in the parent state. Also reject ranking a branch highest simply because it prints a later selected OK run or confident success message while providing less evidence about default merging and LEVEL_TAGS assignment semantics. The dominant public contract is dynamic Message.level_tag resolution under @override_settings; LEVEL_TAGS compatibility is secondary and should be credited only to the extent the visible implementation or tests show real legacy behavior.

Abstention boundary: if the visible parent/continuation state does not show the level_tag source, the LEVEL_TAGS replacement semantics, or behavioral outputs for override/default restoration, do not infer correctness from summaries or intent. If all candidate continuations share the inherited dynamic level_tag change and none shows distinguishable proxy/default-merge/assignment evidence or meaningful test outcomes, treat them as tied or unobservable rather than preferring the branch with the loudest final success text.

experiences.title: Pytest mark expression: escape reserved-looking identifiers, do not convert them to Python literals
experiences.description: Use this when judging paused trajectories for the pytest `Expression.compile('False')` Python 3.8+ AST compiler crash. The decisive issue is not merely making `compile()` accept `True`, `False`, or `None`; it is preserving pytest mark-expression identifier lookup semantics while avoiding forbidden raw Python AST names.
experiences.context: Activation conditions: the prompt or visible trajectory shows `Expression.compile('False')` crashing or raising `ValueError: identifier field can't represent 'False' constant`, references Python 3.8+ debug/non-debug AST compiler behavior, and inspects `src/_pytest/mark/expression.py`, especially `not_expr`, `ast.Name`, `ast.NameConstant`/`ast.Constant`, or `MatcherAdapter`. The grammar visible in the file treats `True`, `False`, and `None` as identifier spellings in the custom expression language, resolved through the matcher mapping during evaluation. A local Python 3.10 non-debug `ValueError` is relevant evidence for the same compiler rejection even if the original report describes a debug-build abort.
experiences.experience:
Core rule: reject the misleading rubric or judge bias that says the bug is simply that `True`, `False`, and `None` are parsed as `ast.Name` and should be converted to `ast.Constant` literals. That interpretation fixes host-AST compilation but can break pytest’s own expression language. A correct implementation may prefix, escape, wrap, or otherwise represent these spellings so the Python compiler accepts the AST, but evaluation must still call the matcher for the original identifier string. Do not require one exact patch shape; equivalent implementations are valid if they satisfy this contract.

Decisive positive evidence: source inspection or a visible diff shows the identifier path no longer emits raw `ast.Name('True'/'False'/'None')` while still routing those names through `MatcherAdapter` or an equivalent lookup; the implementation escapes or renames AST identifiers and unescapes them before calling the matcher, or otherwise preserves matcher dispatch. Strong tests are discriminating tests, not truth-table coincidences: for example, `Expression.compile('False').evaluate(lambda name: True)` should return true if `False` is still an identifier; `Expression.compile('True').evaluate(lambda name: False)` should return false; `Expression.compile('None').evaluate(lambda name: True)` should return true rather than `None`; and a matcher that records keys should observe `'True'`, `'False'`, or `'None'`. Mixed expressions such as `'True and foo'` are useful when they prove both reserved-looking and ordinary identifiers use the same lookup semantics. It is also positive when a trajectory explicitly realizes that an earlier literal-conversion patch was wrong and then changes the implementation to preserve identifier semantics; judge the latest visible state, while preserving uncertainty if the final code is not shown.

Contradictory evidence: a patch that branches on `ident.value == 'True'`, `'False'`, or `'None'` and returns `ast.Constant(True)`, `ast.Constant(False)`, or `ast.Constant(None)` for those tokens is evidence against semantic correctness unless it separately proves matcher lookup is still performed. Outputs such as `False evaluates to: False`, `True evaluates to: True`, `None evaluates to: None`, `True and False evaluates to: False`, or `not False evaluates to: True` are weak or contradictory when they are presented as final validation, because they are exactly what Python literals would do. Likewise, saying that these tokens are “actual boolean constants,” validating only that `Expression.compile('False')` succeeds, or testing only a normal identifier such as `foo` does not prove the required behavior. Failed attempts to install or run the broader test suite do not outweigh a semantic violation.

Close-looking exclusions: `Expression.compile('False')` followed by evaluation with `lambda x: False` is not discriminating, because both a literal `False` and a matcher-returned `False` produce the same output. `Expression.compile('True')` with `lambda x: True` is similarly non-discriminating. Merely checking for `ast.Constant` availability, adding version guards, or replacing `NameConstant` for the empty-expression case is adjacent but not enough. A trajectory that only reproduces the current interpreter’s `ValueError` has located the compatibility symptom, not the correct project-language fix.

Abstention boundary: if the paused view is truncated after a file-change summary, a patch script, or mid-debugging commands and does not show the settled code or a discriminating matcher test, do not infer full correctness from diff size or from compilation success. Award partial diagnostic credit for locating `not_expr`/`MatcherAdapter` and for recognizing the identifier-vs-literal problem, but reserve top credit for visible evidence that the final implementation both compiles on Python 3.8+ behavior and preserves matcher-based identifier semantics for `True`, `False`, and `None`.

experiences.title: Second manual correction: Do Not Treat make_model_tuple/App-Registry Speculation as Decisive for Mixed-Case App Lazy References
experiences.description:
SECOND-PASS MANDATORY RULE: Prioritize the causal make_model_tuple and app-label normalization mismatch over command volume or early file contact.

Positive visible evidence: Concrete registry-key and mixed-case app-label normalization chain.
Contradictory or insufficient visible evidence: Serializer or autodetector browsing without the registry mismatch.

For the Django mixed-case app-name ForeignKey task, a continuation should not be ranked highest merely because it confidently names make_model_tuple or app_configs as the cause. The visible prompt uses a class ForeignKey, not a lower-case string reference, so a strong diagnosis must explain how Django generated the lower-case lazy reference from a mixed-case installed app. Without reproduction, patch, or tracing through relation deconstruction/migration state/model option labels, this is only partial exploration.
experiences.context: The task reports a lazy-reference error: a field in app DJ_RegLogin refers to 'dj_reglogin.category', but app 'dj_reglogin' is not installed. The visible user model defines category = models.ForeignKey(Category, on_delete=models.CASCADE), i.e. a class reference in the same app, while INSTALLED_APPS contains 'DJ_RegLogin'. In the paused trajectories, no continuation has changed files or shown a passing reproduction. Several branches inspect model_checks.py, apps/registry.py, fields/related.py, and django/db/models/utils.py; one branch states that make_model_tuple does not normalize app_label and that app_configs uses the mixed-case key, but it has not traced why the class ForeignKey became the lower-case string 'dj_reglogin.category'.
experiences.experience:
Second manual correction after inspecting the failed generated rubric and evidence-first scores:
Prioritize the causal make_model_tuple and app-label normalization mismatch over command volume or early file contact.

Credit only this visible evidence: Concrete registry-key and mixed-case app-label normalization chain.
Reject or cap this visible evidence: Serializer or autodetector browsing without the registry mismatch.
Abstain when: Keep branches tied if no causal normalization difference is visible.

Do not let another retrieved experience replace this task-specific rule with a generic process proxy.

Activation: Apply this when judging paused pre-patch diagnosis for the mixed-case Django app-name ForeignKey issue, especially when branches have no diff, no successful reproduction, and only source exploration around lazy references, app registry lookup, related fields, or make_model_tuple.

Decisive positive evidence: Prefer a continuation that notices the prompt’s ForeignKey is a class reference (ForeignKey(Category)), not a user-written lower-case string, and therefore traces or proposes tracing the path that serializes/deconstructs that class relation into a lazy reference. Strong visible signals include inspecting or explicitly naming ForeignKey.deconstruct(), migration ModelState/ProjectState construction, remote_field.model._meta.label_lower, Options.label_lower, or an equivalent code path where the app-label component could be lowercased. A strong diagnosis states the invariant: preserve or correctly match the installed mixed-case app label while still handling model-name normalization, then validate with a mixed-case app containing a class ForeignKey.

Partial positive evidence: Reading model_checks.py app_model_error(), apps.get_app_config(), lazy_model_operation(), resolve_relation(), or make_model_tuple is relevant symptom investigation. It shows the agent is near the lazy-reference machinery, but by itself it does not establish the root cause for this prompt.

Contradictory evidence: A continuation that confidently says “now I understand” and blames make_model_tuple or app_configs mismatch without explaining how Django produced 'dj_reglogin.category' from ForeignKey(Category) has not completed the causal chain. The observation that make_model_tuple lowercases the model name, or that get_app_config is case-sensitive, does not prove that the app label was incorrectly lowercased. Blaming string-reference parsing is especially weak because the visible user code does not pass a string to ForeignKey.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not confuse resolve_relation() behavior for unqualified string relations with the class-reference path shown in the prompt. Do not treat related_name interpolation using cls._meta.app_label.lower() as the reported lazy-reference source unless the trajectory connects it to the failing field reference. Do not treat model_checks.py as the root cause; it formats the pending lazy-operation error after the bad key already exists. A case-insensitive registry lookup or another implementation could be valid, but only if the continuation explains why it preserves app-label semantics and validates the mixed-case class-ForeignKey scenario.

Misleading pattern rejected: Reject the judging bias that rewards a fluent, confident make_model_tuple/app-registry story as a high-quality diagnosis. In this round, that story is incomplete and likely misdirected unless it accounts for the class ForeignKey and the generation of the lower-case lazy reference. Confidence and relevant file names are not substitutes for the missing causal step.

Abstention boundary: If no continuation has reproduced the issue, applied a patch, or traced the class-ForeignKey-to-lowercase-lazy-reference path, do not single out one branch as clearly superior solely for mentioning make_model_tuple or app_configs. Treat such branches as early partial exploration and rank them close together, while reserving higher scores for visible causal tracing, implementation, or validation evidence.

experiences.title: Do not overrank opaque _print_Subs edits over visible AssocOp structural investigation for Subs LaTeX parenthesizing
experiences.description: Activate for the paused SymPy LaTeX Subs parenthesizing task when comparing trajectories that either inspect or rewrite _print_Subs, investigate precedence/parenthesize helpers, or search for AssocOp as the structural basis for wrapping the substituted expression. Score the visible evidence of the solution mechanism, not mere edit activity or file localization.
experiences.context: The visible issue is that LaTeX printing of a Subs expression with an additive body renders the body next to the evaluation bar without grouping, e.g. it should render with explicit parentheses around the substituted expression before the bar. In this paused view, some trajectories investigate precedence values or derivative parenthesization patterns, one trajectory performs an opaque scripted replacement of _print_Subs with no visible diff or validation output, and another trajectory explicitly pivots to locating and understanding AssocOp. The relevant ranking distinction is whether the trajectory is moving toward structural grouping of the Subs body rather than conditional precedence-based formatting or unverifiable text replacement.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions:
- Apply only to the Subs LaTeX parenthesizing task where the visible paused evidence includes solution-direction investigation around sympy/printing/latex.py, precedence.py, _print_Subs, _print_Derivative, parenthesize, or AssocOp.
- Especially apply when a trajectory that merely touches or rewrites _print_Subs appears to be competing with a trajectory that is still investigating AssocOp or structural expression classes.

Decisive positive evidence:
- Strongly favor a trajectory that visibly investigates AssocOp as the structural condition for grouping the Subs body, including commands/thoughts such as searching for `class AssocOp`, locating it in core operations code, and asking which classes inherit from or use AssocOp.
- Further positive evidence includes identifying that additive/multiplicative associative bodies need grouping before the evaluation bar, or planning/implementing wrapping in the actual _print_Subs rendering path based on expression structure rather than on precedence comparison.
- A direct _print_Subs implementation is also valid if the visible diff or validation output proves the correct rendered behavior. Do not require the literal name AssocOp if the visible implementation equivalently groups the relevant expression structures and preserves appropriate output for non-problematic bodies.

Contradictory evidence:
- Treat as weak or negative a trajectory that focuses on precedence values such as Subs having precedence 1000 while Add has lower precedence, or studies _print_Derivative/parenthesize with PRECEDENCE['Mul'] as the apparent solution pattern. That line of investigation points toward conditional precedence formatting, which is the misleading approach here.
- Treat reproduction-only work, dependency installation, or checking the current LaTeX output as insufficient once other trajectories contain mechanism evidence.
- Treat an opaque scripted replacement of _print_Subs as non-decisive when the visible view does not show the new method body, a diff, or a post-change LaTeX output. A printed `Done` from a replacement script is not evidence that the correct structural wrapping was implemented.

Close-looking exclusions:
- Do not give high credit merely for opening _print_Subs or for knowing the likely file location. Localization is not the same as the correct wrapping mechanism.
- Do not penalize a trajectory for first searching for AssocOp in the wrong file if it then searches the codebase and finds the class definition.
- Do not count checking _print_Limit or other nearby printer methods as positive by itself; it is only useful if followed by structural reasoning about the Subs body.
- Do not treat expression-tree inspection or tests of standalone Subs(Add), Subs(Mul), and Subs(Pow) as decisive unless the trajectory draws the structural conclusion or implements/verifies the corrected rendering.
- Do not penalize brief precedence exploration if the trajectory later pivots clearly to structural wrapping.

Misleading rubric/bias to reject:
- Explicitly reject the bias that an attempted edit or scripted replacement of _print_Subs should outrank a trajectory visibly investigating AssocOp. In this paused view, an unverifiable edit with hidden/truncated replacement content is weaker than visible evidence that the agent is identifying the structural class mechanism needed for a correct fix.
- Also reject the rubric shortcut that treats `_print_Subs return-format inspection` as automatically equivalent to correct explicit wrapping. It is high-value only when the visible evidence shows the actual wrapping rule or final output, not when the changed method body is absent from view.

Abstention boundary:
- If the visible trajectory contains only setup, reproduction, or file browsing with no mechanism direction, keep the score low-to-middle rather than inferring future success.
- If a trajectory has an opaque edit but no visible diff or validation, do not assign a top score; preserve uncertainty.
- If multiple trajectories visibly implement or validate equivalent correct structural grouping in _print_Subs, preserve them as equivalent rather than preferring a particular internal spelling.

experiences.title: Second manual correction: Priority visible-state rule: Test suite regression discovery must outweigh manual HTML verification breadth when ranking autodoc_typehints description-mode fix continuations
experiences.description:
SECOND-PASS MANDATORY RULE: Exact regression execution plus fixture localization is one evidence class; wording detail alone cannot produce a unique winner.

Positive visible evidence: Exact failing test and documented-init fixture inspection.
Contradictory or insufficient visible evidence: Broad HTML checks without the exact configuration test.

MANDATORY RULE: A legacy overfit card changed tie-aware selection using evidence already present in this exact visible trajectory. Its text is retained only as a starting point and must pass the standard recall@6 gate again.

Background: Retrieve when evaluating continuations that verify a fix for autodoc_typehints = "description" causing autoclass to show a spurious return type for classes. Judge whether the continuation ran the actual test suite (test_ext_autodoc_configs.py) and discovered the failing regression test (test_autodoc_typehints_description_with_documented_init), not merely whether it performed multiple manual build-and-check cycles with different autodoc_typehints modes. A continuation that builds and checks HTML output with description, both, and signature modes but never runs test_ext_autodoc_configs.py or only runs it at the very last step with truncated output has not discovered the critical regression: the fix is too broad and removes return type for classes with explicitly documented __init__ methods where it should be preserved.
experiences.context: Applies when the visible task concerns autodoc_typehints = "description" causing autoclass to include a spurious return type from __init__. The parent trajectories already applied a fix to merge_typehints in sphinx/ext/autodoc/typehints.py that skips return type for classes. Continuations are in the verification phase (steps 40-60). The key differentiator is whether the continuation runs test_ext_autodoc_configs.py and discovers the failing test_autodoc_typehints_description_with_documented_init, which tests _ClassWithDocumentedInit — a class with an explicitly documented __init__ where the return type should still appear when :special-members: __init__ is used. A common misleading rubric rewards the continuation for the breadth of manual verification (number of builds, modes tested, HTML grep commands) rather than for discovering the specific regression test failure.
experiences.experience:
Second manual correction after inspecting the failed generated rubric and evidence-first scores:
Exact regression execution plus fixture localization is one evidence class; wording detail alone cannot produce a unique winner.

Credit only this visible evidence: Exact failing test and documented-init fixture inspection.
Reject or cap this visible evidence: Broad HTML checks without the exact configuration test.
Abstain when: Equivalent reproduction without a fix remains tied.

Do not let another retrieved experience replace this task-specific rule with a generic process proxy.

Priority override for rubric generation and weighting:
A legacy overfit card changed tie-aware selection using evidence already present in this exact visible trajectory. Its text is retained only as a starting point and must pass the standard recall@6 gate again.

Reject any generated rubric whose direction, anchors, or weighting contradicts that rule. Apply it only to the matching visible task and stage; otherwise abstain.

Activation: When ranking continuations that verify a fix for the autodoc_typehints = "description" class return type bug, where all continuations show zero changed files (fix already applied by parent) and are in the verification/testing phase. The fix modifies merge_typehints to skip return type for classes, but this is too broad and breaks test_autodoc_typehints_description_with_documented_init.

Decisive positive evidence: A continuation that runs python -m pytest tests/test_ext_autodoc_configs.py and observes FAILED tests/test_ext_autodoc_configs.py::test_autodoc_typehints_description_with_documented_init has discovered the critical regression. This is stronger evidence of fix quality assessment than any amount of manual HTML verification. A continuation that then examines the _ClassWithDocumentedInit test fixture and recognizes that the fix is too broad — it removes return type for all classes, including those with documented __init__ methods where the return type should be preserved — demonstrates the deepest understanding of the issue. A continuation that articulates that the test expects the return type of __init__ to be shown when using :special-members: __init__ and that the fix was too broad has identified the root cause of the regression.

Contradictory evidence: A continuation that performs extensive manual verification — building with description, both, and signature modes, checking HTML output for return types, testing with methods and exception classes — but does not run test_ext_autodoc_configs.py until the very last visible step, or runs it with truncated output, has NOT discovered the regression in the visible prefix. Manual HTML verification cannot catch the _ClassWithDocumentedInit edge case because it requires :special-members: __init__ or equivalent explicit documentation of __init__, which the manual test setup does not include. Do not rank such a continuation above one that found and began investigating the failing test.

Close-looking exclusions: Running test_ext_autodoc.py (which passes with 69 passed, 1 skipped) is NOT equivalent to running test_ext_autodoc_configs.py (which contains the failing test). A continuation that runs test_ext_autodoc.py -k typehint and sees it pass has not validated the fix against the regression test. Similarly, running test_ext_autodoc_autoclass.py (18 passed) or test_ext_autodoc_autofunction.py (13 passed) does not substitute for test_ext_autodoc_configs.py. Do not credit partial test suite execution as if it were full validation. Also, running test_ext_autodoc_configs.py -k typehints at the very last step with truncated output does not demonstrate discovery of the failure unless the FAILED text is explicitly visible in the output.

Misleading rubric rejection: Do not reward a continuation for the QUANTITY of manual verifications (number of builds, number of modes tested, number of HTML grep commands, number of passing test files) when it has not run the specific test suite that contains the regression test. The misleading pattern is: more builds plus more HTML checks plus more passing test files equals more thorough verification. This is false when the test suite contains a specific regression test (test_autodoc_typehints_description_with_documented_init) that manual verification cannot replicate. A continuation with extensive manual build-and-check cycles that never runs test_ext_autodoc_configs.py is LESS thorough than one that runs it once and finds the failure. The judge bias that over-credits visible manual verification breadth while under-crediting test suite regression discovery leads to incorrect branch rankings.

Abstention boundary: If no continuation in the visible state has run test_ext_autodoc_configs.py, do not differentiate based on which tests they DID run or how many manual verifications they performed. If all continuations are still in manual verification mode without any test suite execution, preserve uncertainty. If a continuation has run test_ext_autodoc_configs.py but the output is truncated and the failure is not visible, do not assume it found the failure unless the FAILED text is explicitly visible in the output. Equivalent implementations are acceptable: a continuation that discovers the regression through a different test or through direct examination of the _ClassWithDocumentedInit case without running the exact test name is also credited, as long as it identifies the too-broad-fix problem.

experiences.title: Do Not Treat a BaseConstraint-Only Diff as Complete ValidationError Code Support
experiences.description: For the constraint ValidationError code customization task, a small source diff in the apparent target file is not enough for a high implementation score. The decisive issue is whether the new error-code value is actually accepted, stored, serialized, and passed into every relevant ValidationError raised by constraint validation.
experiences.context: The paused view shows a task asking to allow customization of the code attribute on ValidationError raised by BaseConstraint.validate. Visible exploration identifies that existing constraint validation raises ValidationError(self.get_violation_error_message()) in core constraint code and also in the PostgreSQL constraint file. One continuation has a diff only in django/db/models/constraints.py and reports “BaseConstraint updated successfully,” but its next visible thought says it still needs to update validate methods. The visible pre-edit snippets still show CheckConstraint.__init__ without a code parameter and validate raising ValidationError without a code. Other continuations are exploration or test-script attempts with no source diff, and some validation attempts fail due to missing dependencies.
experiences.experience:
ACTIVATION: Use this experience when judging paused continuations for the constraint ValidationError-code customization task, especially when one branch has a small diff in django/db/models/constraints.py while the visible trajectory does not yet show propagation of the new code into ValidationError calls.

DECISIVE POSITIVE EVIDENCE: Strong implementations should visibly do more than add an attribute to BaseConstraint. Credit evidence that the continuation adds a new violation_error_code-style API to BaseConstraint, stores it, preserves existing violation_error_message behavior, passes it through relevant subclasses such as CheckConstraint and UniqueConstraint, and uses it when raising ValidationError, e.g. by calling ValidationError(message, code=...) or an equivalent helper. Stronger evidence also updates deconstruct()/migration serialization and repr/equality behavior where applicable, and handles the visible PostgreSQL constraint validation path that also raises ValidationError from get_violation_error_message(). Equivalent valid implementations may use a helper like get_violation_error_code(), direct attribute access, or another clean design, as long as the ValidationError.code attribute is actually set when constraints validate.

CONTRADICTORY EVIDENCE: A diff_stat showing only django/db/models/constraints.py changed is not decisive. In the visible changed continuation, the patch script reports only that BaseConstraint was updated, and the next thought explicitly says the validate methods still need to be updated. That is contradictory to a claim of completed feature support because the core behavior requested by the task is the code attribute on raised ValidationError, not merely an initializer parameter. No visible successful validation demonstrates a custom error code. Test scripts that fail with ModuleNotFoundError for asgiref or sqlparse, or scripts that only print existing default violation messages, do not validate the feature.

CLOSE-LOOKING EXCLUSIONS: Do not reward adding another violation_error_message parameter; the task text contains a wording slip, but the requested feature is customization of the ValidationError code. Do not give high credit for exploration-only branches with no changed files, even if they correctly identify ValidationError accepts a code parameter. Do not give high credit for a BaseConstraint-only edit that has not visibly changed CheckConstraint, UniqueConstraint, or the PostgreSQL constraint validation raise site. Do not require one exact patch shape: direct code= passing, a getter helper, or another equivalent implementation are all valid if the raised ValidationError receives the custom code and existing message behavior remains intact.

MISLEADING RUBRIC OR JUDGE BIAS TO REJECT: Reject the bias that “implements core feature changes in correct source files” can be satisfied by any source diff in django/db/models/constraints.py. Correct-file editing is weaker than evidence of behavioral wiring. A branch paused immediately after a BaseConstraint edit, before visible validate-method updates or validation, should not outrank branches merely because it has a diff_stat; it should be scored as partial implementation, not completed feature work.

ABSTENTION BOUNDARY: If the visible patch is truncated so the judge cannot confirm whether ValidationError calls gained a code argument, do not infer completion from the diff_stat alone. Cap the assessment at partial unless later visible evidence shows the propagation and, ideally, a passing focused validation. If a continuation has not yet attempted edits, score it as analysis/exploration rather than implementation. If later visible steps show complete equivalent propagation plus successful validation, this experience should not penalize that implementation.

experiences.title: Second manual correction: Weigh Systematic Error-Chain Tracing and Trajectory Efficiency Over Single-Point Root Cause Specificity When Ranking Pre-Fix Diagnosis Branches
experiences.description:
SECOND-PASS MANDATORY RULE: Task-specific causal localization must dominate directory count, command efficiency, or generic debug-script success.

Positive visible evidence: Direct hyperbolic _eval_is_real to Mod and gcd causal chain.
Contradictory or insufficient visible evidence: Generic substitution or polynomial-conversion tracing without the failing mechanism.

When ranking branches that diagnose a PolynomialError triggered during subs() on expressions with Piecewise and real assumptions, do not over-value a branch that names the most specific-sounding root cause location while under-valuing branches that systematically trace the error through the actual code path across multiple files without wasted steps. A branch that wastes multiple steps on directory navigation and ends with a failed debug script should not rank above branches that efficiently reproduce, locate the error, trace through the polynomial module and subs implementation, and identify the error entry point or mechanism — all without wasted steps.
experiences.context: A SymPy bug where exp(sinh(Piecewise(...)/z)).subs({1: 1.0}) raises PolynomialError: Piecewise generators do not make sense when symbols are real and cache is cleared. Multiple branches diagnosed the issue with divergent approaches: some systematically traced through polytools.py, polyutils.py, basic.py, and exponential.py or mod.py; another jumped directly to _eval_is_real in hyperbolic.py after wasting steps on directory navigation. The judge incorrectly ranked the branch with the most specific root cause articulation highest, despite it having the most wasted steps and a failed final verification script.
experiences.experience:
Second manual correction after inspecting the failed generated rubric and evidence-first scores:
Task-specific causal localization must dominate directory count, command efficiency, or generic debug-script success.

Credit only this visible evidence: Direct hyperbolic _eval_is_real to Mod and gcd causal chain.
Reject or cap this visible evidence: Generic substitution or polynomial-conversion tracing without the failing mechanism.
Abstain when: Do not rank process efficiency as correctness evidence.

Do not let another retrieved experience replace this task-specific rule with a generic process proxy.

Activation: When ranking pre-implementation diagnosis branches for a SymPy error triggered during subs() that involves polynomial conversion failing on Piecewise expressions, and branches show divergent approaches — some systematically tracing through multiple files, others jumping to a specific method — and divergent levels of wasted steps.

Positive evidence (systematic error-chain tracing without wasted steps): A branch that (1) reproduces the issue successfully within the first few steps without extensive directory navigation, (2) locates the error message in polytools.py via grep, (3) traces through _parallel_dict_from_expr in polyutils.py to understand how generators are determined, (4) examines the subs method in basic.py to understand the substitution mechanism, (5) creates a debug script with full traceback that succeeds (returncode 0) to identify the entry point of the error chain (e.g., exp.eval() checking arg.is_zero triggering assumption queries leading to polynomial conversion), and (6) begins examining the specific file where the entry point occurs (e.g., exponential.py). All visible commands are productive: reproduction, grep, sed, cat, and python execution all advance the diagnosis. No steps are wasted on directory navigation.

Positive evidence (mechanism tracing through GCD/Mod path): A branch that reproduces the issue, locates the error, traces through callers of parallel_poly_from_expr, examines _eval_subs in polytools.py, runs a traceback script that succeeds (returncode 0), traces through the gcd function in polytools.py, and examines the Mod class in mod.py. Each step advances understanding of how the error propagates through the codebase. No steps are wasted on directory navigation.

Contradictory evidence (specific root cause with wasted steps and failed verification): A branch that articulates a specific root cause (e.g., 'the error occurs in _eval_is_real of hyperbolic functions which computes (im % pi).is_zero leading to Mod → gcd → PolynomialError') and examines the hyperbolic.py code, BUT wastes multiple steps on directory navigation (trying /root, running find / -name sympy, multiple ls and cd commands before locating the repository, creating files in the wrong directory) and has a failed debug script at the end of its trajectory (returncode 1) — should not rank above branches that systematically traced the error without wasted steps. The specific articulation is genuine diagnostic progress, but the wasted steps reduce trajectory efficiency and the failed debug script indicates incomplete verification.

Close-looking exclusion: Do not conflate 'names the most specific method' with 'best diagnosis.' A branch that identifies _eval_is_real in hyperbolic.py as the root cause location has identified a valid fix target, but a branch that traces from exp.eval() → arg.is_zero → assumption queries → polynomial conversion has identified the ENTRY POINT of the error chain, which is equally valuable for understanding why subs triggers the error. A branch that traces through gcd and Mod has identified the MECHANISM. All three are valid diagnostic approaches; the differentiator is systematic tracing without wasted steps and successful verification, not specificity of the named location.

Close-looking exclusion: Do not penalize a branch for not naming the exact method if it has traced through more of the actual code path. A branch that examines polyutils.py, basic.py subs, and exponential.py has traced through more of the error chain than one that jumps directly to hyperbolic.py, even if the latter names a more specific method. The depth and breadth of code path tracing is a positive signal independent of whether the final root cause location is named with maximum specificity.

Close-looking exclusion: Do not treat a failed debug script (returncode 1) as equivalent to a successful one (returncode 0). A branch whose final debug script errors has incomplete verification, while a branch whose debug script succeeds has confirmed its hypothesis. This difference should factor into the ranking. Also count wasted steps: a branch that spends 7+ steps on directory navigation (trying wrong paths, running find, creating files in wrong locations) has less effective diagnostic time than one that locates the repository immediately.

Misleading pattern rejection: The pattern 'branch that articulates the most specific root cause location (naming exact method and expression) should rank highest' is misleading when that branch wasted steps on directory navigation and had a failed debug script. Score based on the combination of (1) successful reproduction, (2) error location identification, (3) systematic tracing through the codebase across multiple relevant files, (4) identification of the error mechanism or entry point, (5) absence of wasted steps on navigation, and (6) successful verification with returncode 0 — not on the specificity of the root cause articulation alone. A branch that traces through 5+ relevant files without wasted steps and identifies the error entry point should rank at least as high as one that names a specific method but wasted 7+ steps on navigation and failed to verify.

Abstention boundary: If all branches show only reproduction and error message location without any tracing through the codebase, do not attempt to distinguish diagnosis quality beyond reproduction success. If all branches wasted steps on navigation or all had failed debug scripts, the differentiator collapses and ranking should be based on reproduction and error location alone. This experience applies only when branches show divergent approaches to tracing the error chain and divergent levels of wasted steps and verification success.

experiences.title: Rank post-failure diagnosis and domain-index tracing above adapter-warning grep for special toctree pages
experiences.description: For the Sphinx toctree generated-page issue, do not rank a branch highly merely because it has a directive-only patch, a build that still emits the same warnings, and then greps the toctree adapter warning string. At this paused view, stronger visible evidence is either (1) explicitly reacting to the failed build by debugging why the current directive condition still mismatches normalized docnames, or (2) tracing the generated index/domain-index mechanism behind modindex/py-modindex rather than treating genindex/modindex/search as ordinary source documents.
experiences.context: The visible task is to allow `genindex`, `modindex`, and `search` entries in a Sphinx `.. toctree::` without nonexisting-document warnings. The paused continuations include directive-only patches whose validation builds still say `build succeeded, 9 warnings`, branches that only browse builder/environment files, a branch that greps the adapter warning line after the failed build, a branch that acknowledges the warnings and inspects `docname_join`, and a branch that follows the Python/domain index special-target path (`PythonModuleIndex`, `sphinx/domains/__init__.py` special hyperlink target such as `py-modindex`).
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply this only for the visible Sphinx toctree issue involving generated pages such as `genindex`, `modindex`, and `search`, at the paused exploration/implementation boundary where no continuation has yet shown a complete validated fix. It is especially relevant when one continuation is being overcredited for `sphinx/directives/other.py` edits plus a persistent-warning build plus adapter grep, while other continuations show either post-failure debugging of the directive comparison or tracing of generated domain index targets.

Decisive positive evidence: Give materially higher trajectory credit to a continuation that, after a directive-level patch, runs an HTML build, sees that warnings persist, explicitly states that the warnings are still appearing, and immediately investigates why the docname comparison may be wrong by inspecting `docname_join` or equivalent normalization logic. This is not completion, but it is stronger visible evidence than passively grepping the second warning line because the agent is using validation failure to refine the actual condition being patched. Also give strong diagnostic credit to a continuation that traces `modindex` through Sphinx’s domain-index machinery, such as inspecting `PythonModuleIndex` and finding the `sphinx/domains/__init__.py` special hyperlink target comment for index pages like `py-modindex`; that path is relevant because these entries are generated/index targets rather than source documents.

Contradictory evidence: A one-file directive patch followed by `build succeeded, 9 warnings` is still incomplete. If the next visible actions are only `sed`/`grep` around `sphinx/environment/adapters/toctree.py` or the literal `toctree contains reference to nonexisting document` string, with no explanation of adapter behavior, no normalized-docname diagnosis, and no generated-page availability model, do not rank that branch above the more diagnostic alternatives. The Sphinx process exit code and phrase `build succeeded` are not validation success when the output explicitly reports warnings. Similarly, broad browsing of `found_docs`, generic builder hooks, or package installation/reproduction without a concrete connection to generated-page validation is weak.

Close-looking exclusions: Finding `HTMLBuilder.hasdoc` with `search`, `genindex`, and `get_builder_config('use_index', 'html')` is relevant, but in this paused view it is not by itself a fix strategy if the agent then only says the directive does not recognize the pages and proceeds to create a test. Looking at `sphinx/directives/other.py` is close, but a hardcoded allow-list that still produces warnings is not enough. Looking at `sphinx/environment/adapters/toctree.py` is close, but merely finding or failing to find a string in that file is not equivalent to understanding how to resolve generated pages. Looking at standard-domain references is close, but the stronger special-index evidence is connecting `modindex` to the domain-index/special-target mechanism such as `py-modindex`.

Misleading rubric or judge-bias rejection: Explicitly reject the rubric interpretation that `directive-level patch + ran build + identified the second validation location` deserves strong credit when the build still reports the same warnings and the only second-location evidence is adapter grep/sed. Also reject the opposite overcorrection that treats every directive-only branch with persistent warnings as equally bad: a branch that acknowledges the failed validation and investigates the concrete docname-normalization mismatch is visibly more promising than one that ignores the implication of the warnings or only searches for another warning line. Preserve equivalent valid implementations: do not require the exact helper name `docname_join` or the exact file `domains/__init__.py` if a continuation otherwise identifies the same normalized-docname or generated domain-index availability issue, or later implements a builder-aware mechanism that satisfies the observable behavior.

Abstention boundary: Do not use this experience to declare completion. If a later visible continuation modifies both necessary validation paths or otherwise implements a builder-aware/generated-page-aware solution and validates that the relevant warnings disappear while real missing documents still warn, that concrete implementation supersedes this paused-state ranking rule. If none of the visible continuations either diagnoses the failed directive comparison after warnings or traces generated domain-index targets, keep them in an incomplete band and do not choose a top branch solely because it has a non-empty patch, a zero exit code, or an adapter-file grep.

experiences.title: For mixed FiniteSet–Interval Complement, exact passing runtime validation outranks visible-but-failing edit attempts
experiences.description: Retrieve when judging a paused SymPy trajectory for the issue where `Complement(FiniteSet(x, y, 2), Interval(-10, 10))` should simplify by removing the numeric element inside the interval while preserving symbolic elements. If the paused view shows one branch running the exact reported expression from the active source tree and getting `{x, y}` as a `FiniteSet`, rank that branch above branches that show apparent source edits, patch scripts, or method snippets but whose subsequent tests still return an unevaluated `Complement` or other wrong form.
experiences.context: In this round, the visible summaries may show no changed-file metadata even when branches have executed edit commands, and the displayed continuation window may begin after important prior work. Therefore, do not use `changed_files: None` or `current_patch_chars: 0` as a hard negative when the visible runtime behavior directly validates the reported issue. Conversely, do not favor an apparent edit to `FiniteSet._complement`, `Interval._complement`, or nearby complement logic when the very next visible command demonstrates that the issue still fails. The decisive question in this paused view is whether the exact mixed-symbol-and-number finite-set complement is now evaluated to the correct finite set, not whether the judge can see a clean patch summary.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: apply this experience when the task is the SymPy mixed `FiniteSet`/`Interval` complement bug and the paused view contains some combination of method inspection, edit attempts around complement handling, environment compatibility work, and runtime checks of `Complement(FiniteSet(x, y, 2), Interval(-10, 10))` or `a - b`.

Decisive positive evidence: strongly credit a branch that runs from the intended working directory or explicitly inserts the active source path, imports `FiniteSet`, `Interval`, `Complement`, and `symbols`, constructs `x, y`, `a = FiniteSet(x, y, 2)`, `b = Interval(-10, 10)`, and shows `Result: {x, y}`. Additional confirmation such as `Result type: <class 'sympy.sets.sets.FiniteSet'>`, `Result args: (x, y)`, or `a - b: {x, y}` makes this the strongest visible evidence, even if no source edit is visible in the summary. Also credit supporting semantic probes showing `b.contains(2)` is `True` while `b.contains(x)` and `b.contains(y)` remain symbolic/unknown, because that matches the required filtering behavior.

Decisive contradictory evidence: downgrade branches whose own visible tests still show `Result: Complement({x, y}, Interval(-10, 10))` when `{x, y}` is expected, or produce forms such as `Union(Complement({x, y}, Interval(-10, 10)), {100})` where symbolic elements remain wrapped in an unevaluated complement. A message such as “Patch applied successfully,” a source snippet with a promising comment, or a replacement script is contradicted if the subsequent exact test still fails. Likewise, if direct calls such as `fs._complement(interval)` produce interval-complement unions or otherwise do not correspond to the desired finite-set result, that is not a working fix.

Close-looking exclusions: do not treat merely reading `Complement.reduce`, `FiniteSet._complement`, or `Interval._complement` as implementation success. Do not treat environment compatibility edits, such as `collections.abc` migrations, as evidence that the complement bug is fixed unless followed by the exact complement check succeeding. Do not require that the visible implementation be in only one named method; an equivalent valid implementation may live in `FiniteSet._complement`, `Interval._complement`, `Complement.reduce`, or another appropriate set-operation path, provided the observed behavior correctly removes numeric members known to be in the interval and preserves elements whose membership cannot be decided. Do not over-penalize a branch solely because the summary lacks changed-file metadata when runtime validation proves the behavior.

Misleading rubric or judge bias to reject: reject any rubric that hard-gates top ranking on visible target-method edits or patch metadata while ignoring exact successful runtime output. Also reject the opposite bias of ranking apparent edit activity above a branch that demonstrates the exact reported expression now returns `{x, y}` as a finite set. In this paused view, a visible failing test after an edit is stronger evidence than the edit itself.

Abstention boundary: if no branch shows the exact reported expression or an equivalent `a - b` check succeeding, and the view contains only code reading, verbal root-cause analysis, or unvalidated edit attempts, do not confidently select a top branch based on eloquence or edit location alone. Preserve uncertainty and rank only by concrete, non-contradicted progress toward the required finite-set filtering semantics.

experiences.title: Preserve the case-only glossary reproducer; do not rank downstream glossary renames above Sphinx behavior evidence
experiences.description: For the glossary duplicate-term task where the prompt asks whether `MySQL != mysql`, evaluate whether a continuation preserves the two case-distinct glossary terms and investigates or changes Sphinx behavior. Do not credit renaming the reporter’s lowercase glossary entry as the correct fix merely because the documentation build later succeeds.
experiences.context: The visible prompt reports a Sphinx warning for glossary entries that differ only by case and explicitly states the expected behavior as `MySQL != mysql`. In the paused view, several continuations edit `docs/glossary.rst` to rename the lowercase `mysql` entry to `mysql (PHP extension)` and then build successfully. Another visible continuation instead changes the Sphinx version used for the reporter documentation and runs the build without showing any glossary edit. The ranking failure is caused by a rubric that treats the downstream glossary rename as the implementation target, even though that removes the reported case-only duplicate rather than fixing or isolating Sphinx’s handling of case-distinct glossary terms.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions:
- Apply when the task is the Sphinx glossary duplicate-term issue and the prompt’s expected behavior says `MySQL != mysql` or otherwise indicates that case-only-different glossary terms should be valid.
- Apply when visible continuations include downstream documentation edits such as changing the lowercase `mysql` glossary entry to `mysql (PHP extension)`, compared against continuations that preserve the reported glossary terms while testing Sphinx behavior, Sphinx versions, or Sphinx internals.

Decisive positive evidence:
- Strongly credit a continuation that keeps the reported case-distinct glossary entries intact and investigates the Sphinx-side behavior that decides whether they are duplicates.
- Visible positive evidence includes using a different Sphinx version on the reporter documentation and running `make html` successfully without any visible glossary diff or removal of the lowercase `mysql` term. In this paused view, the sequence installing `Sphinx==5.0.0` in the documentation directory followed by `make html` with return code 0 is meaningful because it tests whether the original case-only duplicate is accepted under changed Sphinx behavior rather than deleting the reproducer.
- Equivalent valid implementations remain acceptable: modifying Sphinx’s glossary/domain duplicate detection, adding a regression case with both `MySQL` and `mysql` unchanged, adjusting duplicate-key normalization so exact-case-distinct terms can coexist, or selecting/pinning a Sphinx version only when the continuation connects that version choice to preserving the original case-distinct terms and eliminating the warning.

Contradictory evidence:
- A continuation that says the solution is to make the terms unique by renaming `mysql` to `mysql (PHP extension)` is contradicting the prompt’s expected behavior. It treats the reporter’s input as invalid instead of fixing or isolating Sphinx’s case handling.
- A visible command such as `sed -i ... mysql (PHP extension) ...`, a diff showing `-    mysql` and `+    mysql (PHP extension)`, or a check that `grep -n "^    mysql$"` no longer finds the lowercase term is evidence that the reproducer was removed.
- A successful documentation build after that rename, including a build that reports success and no duplicate warning, validates only the workaround. It does not show that Sphinx now permits both `MySQL` and `mysql` unchanged.

Close-looking exclusions:
- Do not treat reference searches for `:term:` usages or checks for lowercase `mysql` references as progress toward the Sphinx fix when they are being used to support a rename workaround.
- Do not treat a clean build after renaming the glossary entry as stronger than a build that preserves the original terms under different Sphinx behavior. The key question is whether the case-only duplicate remains present.
- Do not dismiss a no-source-diff continuation as having no useful evidence when the visible commands show it is testing Sphinx version behavior on the unchanged reporter documentation. In this task shape, absence of a glossary diff can be positive because it preserves the reproducer.
- Conversely, merely installing a Sphinx version that fails for an unrelated import/runtime reason is not enough by itself. It becomes useful evidence only when followed by a successful build or a clear diagnosis tied to case-distinct glossary handling.

Observed misleading rubric or judge bias to reject:
- Explicitly reject any rubric that says the minimal correct fix is to rename `mysql` to `mysql (PHP extension)` in `docs/glossary.rst`. That rubric rewards a downstream workaround and erases the exact `MySQL` versus `mysql` case that the prompt asks Sphinx to allow.
- Also reject the bias that build success after removing the lowercase glossary term proves correctness. It proves only that the offending input was changed.

Abstention boundary:
- If no visible continuation either preserves both case-distinct terms while demonstrating a successful Sphinx behavior/version path, or investigates/changes Sphinx’s duplicate-term logic with a concrete plan, do not assign maximum credit to any branch. Prefer low or partial scores rather than ranking a downstream glossary rename as correct.
- If a continuation shows only a successful command with no visible indication that the original `MySQL` and `mysql` entries were preserved, and no Sphinx-side reasoning, do not infer full correctness. The decisive boundary is preserved case-distinct input plus Sphinx-side behavior evidence.

experiences.title: Require Routed TemplateView Handoff Validation, Not Direct LazyDict Helper Success
experiences.description: When judging the TemplateView URL-kwargs SimpleLazyObject crash, do not treat direct calls to the URL-kwargs wrapper dictionary as full validation. The visible TemplateView code passes wrapped kwargs through `get_context_data(**context_kwargs)`, so a fix must show the real slug reaches the user override and ORM through that handoff, or otherwise provide a correct code-level mechanism such as field preparation handling. Extra dictionary-method wrapper tests are optional and must not dominate the ranking.
experiences.context: The paused view shows the relevant TemplateView flow: URL kwargs are wrapped by `_wrap_url_kwargs_with_deprecation_warning(kwargs)` and then passed with `context = self.get_context_data(**context_kwargs)`. The original failure is reproduced when `kwargs.get('offer_slug')` yields a `SimpleLazyObject` that SQLite cannot bind; converting to `str()` succeeds. Several continuations direct-test `_wrap_url_kwargs_with_deprecation_warning({'offer_slug': 'test-slug'}).get('offer_slug')` after introducing a custom dictionary and show `Value from .get(): test-slug`, `Type from .get(): <class 'str'>`, and ORM success. That is only helper-level evidence unless the actual `**context_kwargs` handoff into `get_context_data()` is exercised. Other continuations inspect the ORM field preparation path and observe that `Field.get_prep_value()` handles `Promise` but not `SimpleLazyObject`, which is strong causal diagnosis for an equivalent valid implementation.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply when scoring paused continuations for the TemplateView URL-kwargs SimpleLazyObject issue, especially when a branch edits `_wrap_url_kwargs_with_deprecation_warning()` or introduces a custom dict-like wrapper, and the visible source flow includes `context_kwargs = _wrap_url_kwargs_with_deprecation_warning(kwargs)` followed by `self.get_context_data(**context_kwargs)`.

Decisive positive evidence: The strongest validation is a post-edit script that exercises the actual TemplateView handoff, not merely the helper object. Good examples include invoking an `OfferView`/`TemplateView` through `get()` or `as_view()` with `offer_slug='test-slug'`, or at minimum calling `view.get_context_data(**_wrap_url_kwargs_with_deprecation_warning({'offer_slug': 'test-slug'}))` where the overridden `get_context_data()` itself does `offer_slug = kwargs.get('offer_slug')` and then `get_object_or_404(Account, slug=offer_slug)`. Decisive output shows the value inside the user override is the real slug, e.g. `test-slug`, type `str` or otherwise non-lazy resolved value, `Is SimpleLazyObject: False`, and `Success: Account object (1)`. Also credit evidence that the existing deprecation warning still fires on supported access paths, such as a fresh `.get()` or `[]` access capturing `RemovedInDjango40Warning`. Strong diagnosis without a patch includes locating `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py` around `Field.get_prep_value()`, observing that it already coerces `Promise`, and explaining that `SimpleLazyObject` is not covered before database binding.

Preserve equivalent implementations: A valid solution need not be a custom wrapper in `django/views/generic/base.py`. A fix in URL-kwargs wrapping, field preparation, lazy-object coercion, database parameter preparation, or another appropriate layer can be valid if the visible evidence shows the real slug reaches ORM filtering through the TemplateView path and the deprecation-warning behavior is not obviously broken. Do not require speculative overrides for every dictionary method.

Contradictory evidence: A branch is not validated if the post-edit output still shows `Value from .get(): <object object at ...>`, `Type from .get(): <class 'object'>`, or `No Account matches the given query`; that is the lazy empty sentinel or an otherwise wrong query value, not a fixed slug. A script that directly calls `view.get_context_data(offer_slug='test-slug')` with an ordinary string bypasses the TemplateView wrapping path and cannot validate this bug by itself. Direct helper tests such as `_wrap_url_kwargs_with_deprecation_warning(...).get(...)` returning `str` are useful partial evidence but do not prove the `**context_kwargs` transfer into the user override works. Generic test-runner failures from missing pytest, missing settings, or collection configuration are neutral setup failures, not proof for or against the targeted fix.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not be fooled by a custom dict whose `.get()` and `__getitem__()` work when called directly; the task-level path includes keyword expansion into `get_context_data()`, so the validation must exercise that handoff or an implementation layer that makes the handoff irrelevant. Do not treat iteration/items/values/contains/len tests as decisive edge-case superiority; they may be reasonable supporting checks, but the reported user code only requires supported access to expose the resolved slug while preserving the warning. Do not credit a one-off monkey patch inside `python -c` as a source fix unless the source is visibly updated afterward and the targeted validation is rerun. Be cautious with `_wrapped` inspection after `str(value)` or printing has already forced evaluation; fresh lazy objects can still contain the empty sentinel before setup.

Misleading rubric or judge bias to reject: Reject any rubric that gives near-maximum credit merely for editing `base.py` to add `_LazyDict` plus direct wrapper `.get()`/iteration tests. That overvalues a speculative dictionary wrapper and underchecks the actual TemplateView handoff. Also reject any rule that penalizes field-preparation or database-preparation approaches solely because they are not wrapper-based; the observable invariant is that routed URL kwargs expose the real slug to ORM filtering and warning semantics remain acceptable.

Abstention boundary: If no visible branch validates the actual `get_context_data(**context_kwargs)` or routed `as_view()`/`get()` path after a source edit, do not award full fix-validation credit to any branch based on direct helper tests alone. Score such branches in the partial-implementation or diagnosis range according to visible causal reasoning and patch plausibility. If all branches only reproduce the issue or only direct-test the helper without routed validation, abstain from fine-grained claims of final correctness; do not rank branches primarily by the number of optional dictionary methods they tested.

experiences.title: roc_curve: do not rank all-thresholds-in-[0,1] clipping above the visible np.inf sentinel comparison
experiences.description: For this paused roc_curve threshold task, the strongest visible diagnostic signal is identifying that the local source prepends `thresholds[0] + 1` while an installed implementation prepends `np.inf`. Do not prefer continuations merely because they chase a conditional clip-to-1 workaround or treat `inf` as proof that a fix failed.
experiences.context: The visible prompt concerns `roc_curve` prepending an extra threshold for the `(fpr=0, tpr=0)` point. In the paused view, some continuations inspect `_binary_clf_curve` and the local `roc_curve` code, while one visible path compares the installed package line `thresholds = np.r_[np.inf, thresholds]` with the local source line `thresholds = np.r_[thresholds[0] + 1, thresholds]`. Other visible paths treat a first threshold of `inf` as a failed all-thresholds-within-[0,1] condition or propose `extra_threshold = 1` when scores look like probabilities.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply this experience when judging paused continuations for the roc_curve probability-threshold issue and the visible evidence includes either (a) an installed-vs-local comparison showing `np.inf` in the installed implementation and `thresholds[0] + 1` in the local source, or (b) a continuation treating `inf` as the same failure as the old finite `thresholds[0] + 1` behavior, or pushing a clip-to-1 workaround as the main fix.

Decisive positive evidence: Give strongest credit to a continuation that visibly locates the exact local offending assignment `thresholds = np.r_[thresholds[0] + 1, thresholds]` and also identifies the installed implementation’s contrasting `thresholds = np.r_[np.inf, thresholds]`. This is not distracting version checking: it directly exposes a plausible sentinel-based resolution for the extra ROC threshold. A continuation may also earn meaningful credit by tracing `_binary_clf_curve` to show that `thresholds[0]` is the maximum score and that adding 1 creates a finite threshold above 1 for probability-like scores, but that is less decisive if it then ignores the sentinel evidence.

Contradictory evidence: Explicitly reject the misleading rubric or judge bias that treats `extra_threshold = 1 if thresholds[0] <= 1 else thresholds[0] + 1` as the expert answer solely because the prompt mentions clipping. That workaround is not visibly equivalent unless the continuation also handles the sentinel semantics, including cases where a probability score can equal 1 and the added threshold must still represent the artificial no-positive-predictions point. Also reject the bias that marks a first threshold of `np.inf` from an installed package as a failed local fix merely because `np.inf <= 1` is false. In the visible view, `inf` is evidence of an alternate sentinel implementation, not proof that the old local `+ 1` bug remains. A continuation that tests from a location importing the installed package and then concludes its local change failed because thresholds still start with `inf` should not outrank the continuation that precisely identifies the local-vs-installed assignment difference.

Close-looking exclusions: Inspecting the installed package after local import failures is relevant when it finds the exact `np.inf` threshold-prepend line; do not dismiss it as generic environment exploration. Conversely, running a reproduction that prints `[inf, ...]` from the installed package is not by itself a reproduction of the old local finite-`+1` behavior. Reading `_binary_clf_curve`, showing `thresholds[0] + 1` would be 1.8, or proposing the prompt’s clipping workaround is useful partial diagnosis, but should not be ranked above exact local-line plus installed-sentinel evidence. A visible attempted edit with no reliable diff or with truncated verification should not be assumed to be a correct implementation. Preserve equivalent valid implementations: do not require the literal token `np.inf` if a continuation clearly preserves the out-of-band extra-threshold semantics, but do not treat plain clipping to 1 as equivalent without that reasoning.

Abstention boundary: If the visible view does not show the exact local assignment, does not show the installed `np.inf` assignment, and does not show whether `inf` came from the installed package or the local source, do not infer the correct branch from names, intentions, or command count. If a later visible diff fully implements and validates a different semantically equivalent sentinel strategy, this no-diff paused-prefix experience should yield to direct implementation evidence.

experiences.title: Priority visible-state rule: Contradiction-first judging for xarray HasValues .values guards: Dataset inclusion is not completeness
experiences.description:
MANDATORY RULE: Apply contradiction-first scoring: demote guards containing xr.Dataset, leaving a failing compatibility test, or lacking a durable diff. Unwrap only known array containers such as pandas Series/DataFrame and xarray DataArray/Variable.

Background: Use this experience when judging paused xarray trajectories for the Variable.__setitem__ / DataArray.loc object-assignment bug where arbitrary objects with a .values attribute are coerced. The central correction is to demote direct .values guards that include xr.Dataset, even if they pass the original HasValues script, because the visible trajectory evidence shows Dataset.values is a method rather than array data. Prefer trajectories that restrict unwrapping to known array containers and preserve arbitrary objects.
experiences.context: Activation: the visible task is the xarray Variable.__setitem__ coercion issue, the trajectory has located xarray/core/variable.py and as_compatible_data around the comment 'we don't want nested self-described arrays' and the line data = getattr(data, "values", data), or is applying a guard around that line. The paused view includes visible reproduction output showing bad_indexed.values becomes [5], visible inspection of pandas/xarray .values behavior, and in one branch visible output that Dataset({'a': [1]}).values exists but has type method.
experiences.experience:
Priority override for rubric generation and weighting:
Apply contradiction-first scoring: demote guards containing xr.Dataset, leaving a failing compatibility test, or lacking a durable diff. Unwrap only known array containers such as pandas Series/DataFrame and xarray DataArray/Variable.

Reject any generated rubric whose direction, anchors, or weighting contradicts that rule. Apply it only to the matching visible task and stage; otherwise abstain.

Apply contradiction-first scoring. Decisive positive evidence: a trajectory connects the symptom to the broad getattr(data, "values", data) in as_compatible_data and plans or applies a narrow type-based extraction for known self-described array containers whose .values is actual array-like data for this purpose, such as pandas Series/DataFrame, pandas NDFrame plus any needed xarray DataArray handling, xarray DataArray, or equivalent compatibility types. It should preserve the reported HasValues instance as an object while maintaining legitimate pandas/DataArray conversion behavior. Equivalent valid implementations may use an explicit tuple, a helper predicate, pandas NDFrame plus DataArray, or include legacy pandas panel support; exact spelling is not important if arbitrary .values objects are not coerced and Dataset is not blindly unwrapped.

Contradictory evidence: a visible patch or proposed guard like isinstance(data, (pd.Series, pd.DataFrame, xr.DataArray, xr.Dataset)): data = data.values is not a complete fix and must not receive top implementation credit. The paused view visibly establishes that Dataset.values is a method, so this implementation would convert a Dataset to its mapping-style values method, not array data. Also contradictory are guards that still use getattr/hasattr on arbitrary objects, broad checks that only require a non-callable .values attribute, or any approach that would still coerce the reported HasValues.values = 5. A branch that applies the Dataset-inclusive guard and only shows the original HasValues script passing remains flawed; the passing reproduction does not erase the visible Dataset contradiction. If a branch’s own compatibility/edge test visibly fails after the patch, or the paused summary shows no durable changed file despite an attempted edit, do not treat it as a validated final fix.

Close-looking exclusions: reject the misleading bias that xr.Dataset should be included merely because variable.py imports xarray as xr with a comment mentioning Dataset and DataArray, or because the docstring says pandas or xarray objects should use values. The more specific runtime evidence that Dataset.values is a method is decisive. Do not over-differentiate otherwise equivalent valid fixes based on whether pd.Index appears in the guard, because pd.Index is already handled earlier through NON_NUMPY_SUPPORTED_ARRAY_TYPES before the broad .values line. Extensive pandas MRO, Index, or DataArray exploration is only useful insofar as it leads to a restricted extraction rule; it should not outrank a visible correct implementation, but it can outrank a visibly contradictory Dataset-inclusive implementation.

Abstention boundary: if a paused trajectory has diagnosed the broad .values line but has not yet shown whether it will include or exclude xr.Dataset, preserve uncertainty and score the visible diagnosis rather than assuming success or failure. If no patch content or durable diff is visible, judge root-cause analysis and validation intent, not imagined final code. If a visible patch includes xr.Dataset in a direct data = data.values branch, that is enough contradictory evidence to withhold top credit even when the original minimal reproduction passes.
