experiences.title: Rank type_to_xref discovery in python.py over stringify/restify output inspection for Literal nitpick cross-reference bugs
experiences.description: When evaluating Sphinx trajectories for the Literal nitpick bug where Literal[True] values trigger py:class reference warnings, the decisive localization evidence is finding the type_to_xref function in sphinx/domains/python.py where type strings are converted to pending_xref cross-reference nodes. Branches that only inspect stringify/restify output in sphinx/util/typing.py have diagnostic value but have not reached the fix location. The type_to_xref function shows that None gets reftype='obj' while other values get a different reftype, revealing the root cause and the fix pattern that Literal values need.
experiences.context: Applies to Sphinx autodoc tasks where the reported symptom is that Literal annotation values like True, False are flagged as missing py:class reference targets under nitpick mode. Multiple branches explore sphinx/util/typing.py (stringify/restify), sphinx/ext/autodoc/typehints.py, and sphinx/domains/python.py. The branch that finds type_to_xref in sphinx/domains/python.py and observes the None special case has reached the actual fix location where cross-reference reftypes are determined. A common misleading rubric rewards branches that produce detailed stringify/restify test output showing the stringification mechanism, treating this as the highest evidence tier. That observation is useful diagnostics but does not identify where True is converted to a py:class pending_xref node.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply when the paused view shows pre-implementation exploration for the Sphinx Literal nitpick bug, where the reported symptom is py:class reference target not found for Literal values like True/False. All compared branches have no patch yet. The key ranking question is whether a branch has found the cross-reference creation path in the Python domain.

Decisive positive evidence: A branch that examines sphinx/domains/python.py and finds the type_to_xref function has reached the actual fix location. Visible evidence includes: grep for xref/cross in sphinx/domains/python.py showing type_to_xref at line 83, followed by sed of lines 83-130 showing the function body where None gets reftype='obj' while other values get a different reftype. This function is where type strings are converted to pending_xref nodes, and the None special case demonstrates the exact pattern that Literal values like True/False need. This is stronger localization evidence than any amount of stringify/restify output inspection because it identifies where the cross-reference node is created and where the fix must be applied.

Contradictory evidence: A branch that creates test scripts to inspect stringify and restify output (e.g., discovering that restify produces :obj:`~typing.Literal`\ [True] and stringify produces Literal[True]) has useful diagnostic evidence but has NOT reached the fix location. The stringify/restify functions in sphinx/util/typing.py produce the type string, but the cross-reference node creation happens in type_to_xref in sphinx/domains/python.py. Understanding the string output does not identify where True is converted to a py:class pending_xref node. Do not rank a branch with only stringify/restify output inspection above a branch that found type_to_xref.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not credit reproduction of the nitpick warning alone as sufficient for top ranking — multiple branches reproduce the issue, but only the branch that finds type_to_xref has reached the fix location. Do not credit inspection of sphinx/ext/autodoc/typehints.py (merge_typehints, modify_field_list, augment_descriptions_with_types) as equivalent to finding type_to_xref — the typehints extension processes annotations as strings in field lists, but the cross-reference node creation for signature annotations happens in the Python domain. Do not credit finding _parse_annotation in sphinx/domains/python.py alone without also finding type_to_xref — _parse_annotation calls type_to_xref to create cross-reference nodes, and type_to_xref is where the reftype decision is made. Do not penalize a branch for also exploring stringify/restify — the best branch may explore both, but the decisive evidence is finding type_to_xref.

Misleading rubric rejection: Reject any rubric or judge bias that rewards detailed stringify/restify output inspection as the highest evidence tier. A rubric that ranks a branch with concrete test output showing restify produces :obj:`~typing.Literal`\ [True] above a branch that found type_to_xref in sphinx/domains/python.py is incorrectly prioritizing diagnostic mechanism understanding over fix-location identification. The actual fix must modify the cross-reference creation logic in type_to_xref (or the code that calls it) to handle Literal values differently, not the stringification helpers. The None special case in type_to_xref is the template for the fix — Literal values need similar special treatment to avoid being treated as py:class references.

Preserve equivalent valid implementations: This experience does not forbid later valid fixes that handle Literal values in _parse_annotation, in the typehints extension, or via a different mechanism, provided the implementation actually prevents Literal values from being treated as py:class cross-references. It only corrects early branch ranking when the visible evidence is exploration rather than implementation.

Abstention boundary: If no branch has found type_to_xref or the Python domain cross-reference creation path, do not create a confident ranking based only on which stringification helper was inspected. If a branch has found both type_to_xref AND connected it to the Literal nitpick issue with a concrete fix plan, give it the highest score. If the visible prefix shows investigation of the Python domain but not specifically type_to_xref, preserve uncertainty — the branch may be close to the fix location but has not yet confirmed it.

experiences.title: roc_curve: rank the local positive-infinity sentinel diff above conditional probability clipping and installed-package tests
experiences.description: For this paused roc_curve threshold task, the decisive implementation evidence is a visible local source diff replacing the artificial `thresholds[0] + 1` threshold with an out-of-band positive-infinity sentinel. Do not rank branches higher merely because they force probability-like thresholds to `1.0`, run tests against an installed package path, or show `All thresholds <= 1: True`.
experiences.context: The visible task concerns `roc_curve` adding an extra threshold so the ROC curve starts at `(fpr=0, tpr=0)`. The paused view contains two close-looking approaches: one approach changes the local source line from `thresholds = np.r_[thresholds[0] + 1, thresholds]` to `thresholds = np.r_[np.inf, thresholds]` and later shows a `git diff` plus submission output; another approach uses conditional logic such as `extra_threshold = 1.0` when thresholds appear to be probabilities, repeatedly patches or tests files under `/usr/local/lib/...`, and gets passing manual output from installed-package imports. The judge must distinguish target-source implementation evidence from installed-package validation and must preserve the artificial no-predictions threshold semantics.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply when judging this paused `roc_curve` probability-threshold round and the visible continuations include both (a) a local-source change or diff replacing the `thresholds[0] + 1` prepend with `np.inf` or an equivalent positive-infinity/out-of-band sentinel, and (b) a competing continuation that implements or validates conditional clipping to `1.0` for probability-like scores, especially after copying files into an installed package path or running tests from `/tmp`.

Decisive positive evidence: Rank highest the continuation that visibly modifies the target source line for `roc_curve` so the prepended threshold is `np.inf` (or a semantically equivalent positive-infinity sentinel), verifies it with `git diff`, and submits or prepares a patch containing that source change. Extra credit within the visible evidence may be given for updating the docstring/example from the old `1.8`/`max(y_score)+1` behavior to the infinity sentinel, but the core decisive signal is the local code diff. Manual checks showing `thresholds: [inf, ...]`, `np.isinf(thresholds[0])`, and remaining finite probability thresholds in `[0, 1]` support the diff when they are consistent with the sentinel semantics.

Contradictory evidence: Explicitly reject the misleading rubric or judge bias that treats the prompt’s conditional clipping workaround (`extra_threshold = 1.0` when scores are in `[0, 1]`) as the required or superior solution. A first threshold of `1.0` is not equivalent to an artificial no-predictions sentinel when the maximum probability score can itself be `1.0`; it can duplicate a real decision threshold and lose the out-of-band meaning. Also reject the bias that rewards a branch mainly because it prints `All thresholds <= 1: True` or passes a manual installed-package test. Tests run after editing `/usr/local/lib/...` or after reinstalling packages validate the installed environment, not necessarily the local source change. The prompt’s visible assertion using `np.logical_or(thresholds <= 1, thresholds >= 0)` is also a weak signal because it can pass despite not checking the intended range correctly.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not treat a reproduction from an installed package that already returns `[inf, ...]` as proof that the local source has been fixed; it is strong diagnostic evidence only when followed by a target-source edit or diff. Do not give implementation credit for copying local files into an installed package path, repairing package versions, or repeatedly running tests from `/tmp` if the visible local source remains a conditional clip-to-1 workaround. Do not penalize a valid positive-infinity sentinel simply because `inf <= 1` is false: the first threshold is artificial and represents no predicted positives. Preserve equivalent valid implementations: the literal token `np.inf` is not mandatory if the visible code clearly uses a positive-infinity or otherwise strictly out-of-band sentinel with the same ROC start-point semantics; plain clipping to `1.0` is not equivalent without explicit handling of that sentinel meaning.

Abstention boundary: If the visible continuation lacks a reliable local source diff or source snippet showing the actual `roc_curve` prepend logic, do not infer implementation quality from command count, intentions, or installed-package output. If all visible evidence is only reproduction, package installation, or manual logic snippets without a target-source change, score diagnosis separately and abstain on fix superiority. If a later visible continuation implements and validates a different semantically equivalent out-of-band sentinel strategy in the local source, allow it to compete with the `np.inf` implementation rather than requiring the exact spelling.

experiences.title: Round-specific MiddlewareNotUsed source-ordering judge: adapted value must enter middleware(), not appear only after construction
experiences.description: Use this when ranking paused continuations for the ASGI MiddlewareNotUsed handler-poisoning issue in BaseHandler.load_middleware(). The decisive source question is whether the current middleware constructor receives a mode-adapted handler while the loop state is preserved if MiddlewareNotUsed is raised. A continuation that moves adaptation to after middleware construction is a low-score implementation even if its sync/async smoke scripts print that a chain was built.
experiences.context: The visible paused view concerns Django-style middleware loading where self.adapt_method_mode(), mw_instance = middleware(...), handler, handler_is_async, and except MiddlewareNotUsed interact. Some visible branches run smoke scripts that only report _middleware_chain is not None, and one visible branch shows a post-constructor adapt_method_mode block after mw_instance = middleware(handler), along with output such as sync/async chain-built success and an async_to_sync warning. Other acceptable branches may use a temporary adapted handler or save-and-restore the original handler around the constructor call. Apply this experience only from evidence visible in the paused trajectory: source snippets, diffs, rationale, and command output shown there.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Apply only when the paused view is about BaseHandler.load_middleware() handling MiddlewareNotUsed in sync/async or ASGI middleware loading, and the visible evidence includes source/diff/rationale around self.adapt_method_mode(), mw_instance = middleware(...), handler assignment, or validation scripts for MiddlewareNotUsed chains. Do not apply to unrelated middleware tests or to views where none of the relevant source ordering or validation output is visible.

Decisive positive evidence: Rank highest the continuation whose visible source semantics show that the handler is adapted for the current middleware mode before the middleware factory/constructor is called, and that this adapted value is what the constructor receives. Strong patterns include: adapted_handler = self.adapt_method_mode(...) before the try or before mw_instance = middleware(...), followed by mw_instance = middleware(adapted_handler), with handler updated only after construction succeeds; or a save-original pattern where handler is temporarily adapted before middleware(handler), and the original handler is restored in the MiddlewareNotUsed except path before continue. Equivalent refactors are valid if the constructor receives the adapted callable and a MiddlewareNotUsed exception leaves the previous handler state available for the next middleware. Extra support comes from tests that assert behavior depending on the later middleware receiving the correct sync/async callable, not just from construction succeeding.

Contradictory evidence: Give low implementation credit when the visible diff/source removes the adaptation block from before the constructor and leaves mw_instance = middleware(handler) using the prior unadapted handler, then adds handler = self.adapt_method_mode(...) only after construction or after the mw_instance is None check. This is the diagnosed false-positive behavior: it avoids the side effect by delaying adaptation too far, so the middleware factory is called with the wrong mode. Also penalize rationale that treats "handler adaptation now happens after successful middleware instantiation" as the fix. Smoke output such as "Sync test passed - middleware chain built: True", "Async test passed - middleware chain built: True", or "Async test with async middleware after NotUsed passed: True" does not rescue this source defect when the script only checks _middleware_chain is not None. A warning like "async_to_sync was passed a non-async-marked callable" is not reassuring validation; it is consistent with the adaptation mismatch. Passing simple logging or initialization tests is only secondary regression evidence and cannot outrank wrong constructor ordering.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not require the exact variable name adapted_handler; handler_for_middleware, next_handler, a helper function, or a save/restore structure can be correct. Do not mechanically reject mw_instance = middleware(handler) if the visible lines show handler was already adapted immediately above and will be restored on MiddlewareNotUsed. Do not confuse the final adaptation of the completed middleware chain to the server mode with the per-middleware adaptation that must happen before each constructor call. Do not award top credit to scripts that include a MiddlewareNotUsed class followed by another middleware but only assert that the chain exists; they must verify the later middleware receives or uses the correctly adapted callable to be decisive. Do not treat failed test-load attempts, missing test tools, blank outputs, or grep-only exploration as validation.

Abstention boundary: If the visible code/diff is truncated so the order of self.adapt_method_mode() relative to middleware(...) cannot be determined, assign a middle/uncertain implementation score rather than maximum or minimum. If only test output is visible with no source ordering, treat chain-built messages as weak evidence. If the agent clearly states the correct semantic fix and reports updating the file but the exact changed lines are not visible, give provisional positive credit below a branch whose source visibly proves the constructor receives the adapted handler and the exception path preserves the previous handler.

Explicit bias rejection: Reject any rubric or judging habit that lets "tested both sync and async contexts" or "middleware chain built successfully" dominate the source semantics. For this issue, the implementation ordering is primary: post-constructor adaptation must not outrank a temp-variable or save/restore fix that adapts before middleware construction and preserves state on MiddlewareNotUsed.

experiences.title: Rank real target-error reproduction above unexecuted or simulated binary-payload fixes
experiences.description: For the requests binary payload failure, when the paused view shows partial continuations and no branch has both a visible correct patch and successful execution of the patched real code, do not use a validation-only rubric to flatten exact real-code reproduction to zero. A branch that clears import blockers and reaches the actual UnicodeDecodeError in the real requests code path is stronger partial progress than branches that only apply an unexecuted sed edit or test a locally simulated helper.
experiences.context: Activate this experience for the task where `requests.put(..., data=u"ööö".encode("utf-8"))` fails because `_encode_params` sends bytes to `to_native_string`, which decodes with ASCII on Python 3. The paused view already shows `_encode_params` in `requests/models.py`, `to_native_string` in `requests/utils.py`, `compat.py` where `basestring` includes bytes, and call sites for both URL parameters and request body data. The continuations include Python 3.10 import blockers, attempts to patch `models.py`, local simulated tests, and one continuation that runs `test_binary_payload.py` far enough to hit the actual `UnicodeDecodeError` from `requests/utils.py` rather than failing during import setup.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Use this when judging paused branch prefixes for the binary request-body bug and the visible evidence is incomplete: some branches have plausible source edits but no post-edit execution, some run only simulated helper logic, and at least one branch executes the real code far enough to reproduce the target ASCII decode failure.

Decisive positive evidence: Strong partial-ranking credit should go to a continuation that executes the real installed checkout code, clears the unrelated `collections`/`collections.abc` import blockers, and reaches the specific target failure: a traceback ending in `to_native_string`/`string.decode(encoding)` with `UnicodeDecodeError: 'ascii' codec can't decode byte 0xc3...`. This is not a passing validation, but it proves the branch is exercising the real failure path and has a usable runtime setup for the actual fix. It becomes especially strong when the continuation immediately identifies that `_encode_params` must avoid sending bytes to `to_native_string` and inspects the real `_encode_params` body.

Also positive, but weaker without execution: a visible `models.py` edit that places an `isinstance(data, bytes): return data` branch before the text-string branch, followed by ordinary text handling through `to_native_string` and preserved iterable/key-value URL encoding. This is real patch evidence, but if the branch only creates a test file or shows a source snippet and never runs the patched function, it has not validated the fix.

Contradictory evidence: Do not treat import-setup failures such as `AttributeError: collections.MutableMapping` or `ImportError: cannot import name 'Mapping'` as reproduction of the requested bug. Do not treat a locally redefined `_encode_params` or copied `to_native_string` snippet as validation of the actual modified code. Do not credit a branch that decodes binary body bytes with UTF-8 as fully correct, because arbitrary binary payloads should be preserved as bytes. Do not credit a bytes branch that appears after a broader `(str, bytes)` or `basestring` check, because it is unreachable.

Close-looking exclusions: A return code of zero paired with a printed traceback is not a successful test; read the traceback. If the traceback is the target `UnicodeDecodeError` in the real requests code, it is useful reproduction evidence, not validation evidence. A message like `Fixed!` from a replacement script is not enough unless the resulting `_encode_params` ordering is visible or the real function is executed. `git show` exploration of earlier versions is context only and is not a fix. Diff summaries showing `models.py` changed are weaker than visible branch ordering.

Explicitly reject the misleading validation-only judge bias that an unexecuted sed patch must outrank every branch that has not yet run patched code. In this paused view, if no continuation shows successful execution of the actual patched function, exact real-code reproduction of the target failure after clearing import blockers is a stronger branch-ranking signal than simulated fixed-logic tests or an unexecuted patch. Preserve uncertainty about final correctness: the reproduction branch should not receive full fix credit until the actual bytes-bypass patch is visible or executed, but it should not be scored as equivalent to irrelevant exploration.

Abstention boundary: If truncation hides whether the traceback reached `to_native_string` and the only visible failure is an import/configuration problem, abstain from giving target-reproduction credit. If the actual patched `_encode_params` branch ordering is not visible and the real modified function is not executed, avoid maximum correctness or validation scores. Rank only by visible evidence: real target execution, visible correct source ordering, and preservation of both body bytes and URL-parameter behavior.

experiences.title: RenameModel db_table no-op means skipping all schema_editor work, not just preserving final SQLite table names
experiences.description: For a RenameModel issue where an explicit db_table makes the database operation a no-op, the decisive implementation signal is that RenameModel.database_forwards exits or bypasses the entire schema-editing block when the old and new database table names are unchanged or the table name was explicitly supplied. Do not reward branches primarily for SQLite final-state validation showing the same tables/FKs/M2M tables; that can still miss the reported unnecessary FK/drop-recreate churn because it does not prove schema_editor operations were skipped.
experiences.context: The paused view shows a Django migration task: “RenameModel with db_table should be a noop,” with PostgreSQL FK churn and SQLite table recreation as symptoms of unnecessary RenameModel database work. Visible continuations include: a small patch in django/db/migrations/operations/models.py with 3 insertions; larger patches in the same file with 7 insertions and 6 deletions plus SQLite outputs such as “After rename - Tables: ['custom_table_name'],” PRAGMA foreign_key_list output, and M2M table preservation; several investigation-only continuations with no changed files; and test/setup failures from ad hoc scripts or missing test settings. The key visible risk is mistaking final SQLite schema preservation for proof that RenameModel was a true no-op.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions:
- Apply when the task is specifically RenameModel with an explicitly defined db_table that “should be a noop.”
- Apply when comparing continuations that modify django/db/migrations/operations/models.py against continuations that only investigate, write scripts, or show validation logs.
- Apply especially when a continuation’s validation is SQLite-only and reports final table/FK/M2M state after RenameModel, but does not show that schema_editor.alter_db_table(), schema_editor.alter_field(), or M2M table renaming were not invoked.

Decisive positive evidence:
- The best implementation evidence is a guard in RenameModel.database_forwards that skips the entire database schema operation when the rename would not change the database table. Valid forms include checking old_model._meta.db_table == new_model._meta.db_table, checking that db_table was explicitly supplied via original_attrs/options, or another equivalent condition, provided it prevents all schema_editor work for the explicit-db_table RenameModel path.
- The guard must cover the related-object FK loop and M2M rename loop, not merely the direct alter_db_table call. A true no-op means no database table rename, no related-field alter, and no M2M table rename for the explicit-db_table case.
- Preserving ordinary RenameModel behavior is also important: an auto-generated table name should still rename from the old model table to the new model table.
- Strong validation would spy on schema_editor calls/SQL or otherwise demonstrate zero schema operations for the explicit-db_table case. PostgreSQL validation of no FK drop/recreate is excellent, but a semantically clear backend-agnostic early return can establish correctness even without a visible PostgreSQL run.

Contradictory evidence:
- A patch that only avoids or wraps schema_editor.alter_db_table() but still reaches schema_editor.alter_field() for related objects or the M2M table-renaming block is not a true no-op. This directly misses the PostgreSQL symptom, because unnecessary related-field alters can drop/recreate FK constraints even if the final FK points to the same table.
- SQLite final-state outputs such as “After rename - Tables: ['custom_table_name'],” a PRAGMA foreign_key_list showing the FK references the custom table, or unchanged M2M table names are not decisive. They show the final schema looks plausible, but they do not prove the migration avoided table recreation or FK churn.
- No changed files, only script creation, code inspection, pytest configuration attempts, or a backup file is not an implementation fix.
- Explicitly reject the misleading rubric/judge bias that treats broad SQLite validation coverage or final FK/M2M preservation as more important than the implementation being a full database no-op. Also reject any rubric that requires only “check original_attrs before alter_db_table” while ignoring the downstream related-field and M2M schema operations. Equality of old and new db_table is not a wrong condition if it correctly gates the whole schema-editing block.

Close-looking exclusions:
- A state_forwards-only script showing the ModelState keeps the same db_table is not enough; the bug is in database_forwards/schema_editor behavior.
- An ad hoc failure like OperationalError that a table already exists is likely test setup/isolation contamination unless the output clearly ties it to the implementation. Treat it as neutral rather than evidence the patch is wrong.
- Failed pytest or django test invocations due to missing settings/configuration are neutral validation failures, not evidence against the code.
- A larger rewrite in models.py is not automatically wrong; preserve it if the visible diff or trajectory clearly shows it skips all database schema operations for the explicit-db_table case and preserves normal renames. Conversely, do not promote it solely because it has more SQLite logs.

Abstention boundary:
- If the actual diff content is not visible and only diff_stat plus final-state SQLite output is available, do not make a conclusive semantic claim that a patched continuation is correct. Prefer a plausible patch in the correct file over no patch, but avoid fine-grained ranking between plausible patches unless the view establishes whether the guard covers alter_db_table, related FK alters, and M2M renames.
- If two implementations both visibly make explicit-db_table RenameModel skip all schema_editor work and both preserve ordinary auto-table renames, treat them as equivalent even if one has more validation output.
- If no continuation shows a source patch or enough visible behavior to establish a full no-op, rank validation-only work as incomplete or abstain rather than calling it a completed fix.

experiences.title: Priority visible-state rule: Over-Permissiveness Regression in Security Allowlist Functions Is Veto-Level Evidence Despite Multiple Passing Tests
experiences.description:
MANDATORY RULE: A legacy overfit card changed tie-aware selection using evidence already present in this exact visible trajectory. Its text is retained only as a starting point and must pass the standard recall@6 gate again.

Background: When a continuation fixing a security-relevant allowlist function like ModelAdmin.lookup_allowed() shows a visible test regression where the function returns True/allowed for a lookup that should be blocked (Expected: False), this is veto-level negative evidence that the fix is broken. The judge must rank such a continuation below one with a working fix that passes the full existing test suite, even if the broken fix passes more custom tests.
experiences.context: In a Django ModelAdmin.lookup_allowed() task where a OneToOneField used as a primary key is incorrectly treated as concrete inheritance, one continuation applied a fix that passed the main reproduction test and many custom edge-case tests, but Step 32 showed a visible regression: lookup_allowed returned True for a lookup not in list_filter (Expected: False), meaning the fix was too permissive and broke the security contract. Another continuation applied a working fix, passed its custom tests with no regressions, and ran the full existing modeladmin test suite with all tests showing 'ok'. The judge incorrectly ranked the continuation with the visible regression as the top node, apparently weighting the higher count of passing custom tests over the decisive regression evidence and the stronger full-suite validation in the other continuation.
experiences.experience:
Priority override for rubric generation and weighting:
A legacy overfit card changed tie-aware selection using evidence already present in this exact visible trajectory. Its text is retained only as a starting point and must pass the standard recall@6 gate again.

Reject any generated rubric whose direction, anchors, or weighting contradicts that rule. Apply it only to the matching visible task and stage; otherwise abstain.

ACTIVATION: This experience activates when scoring continuations that fix a security-relevant allowlist or validation function (e.g., ModelAdmin.lookup_allowed, permission checks, input validation gates), and at least one continuation's visible output shows a test regression where the function returns an over-permissive result (True/allowed when the test explicitly expects False/blocked).

POSITIVE EVIDENCE: A continuation that (1) passes the main reproduction test showing the reported bug is fixed, (2) passes edge-case tests for concrete inheritance and regular relations, AND (3) runs the full existing test suite with all tests showing 'ok' status provides the strongest validation evidence. The full existing test suite run is stronger evidence than any number of custom tests because it covers known edge cases and regressions that the agent might not think to test. Visible output from the project test runner showing many tests with 'ok' status is comprehensive validation that the fix does not break existing behavior.

CONTRADICTORY EVIDENCE: A visible test output showing 'Result: True' when 'Expected: False' for a security allowlist function is decisive evidence that the fix is too permissive and has broken the function's core security contract. This single regression is veto-level negative evidence: the function's purpose is to block unauthorized lookups, and a fix that allows blocked lookups has introduced a security vulnerability. This regression outweighs any number of passing custom tests, because the passing tests only show the fix works for cases the agent thought to test, while the regression shows the fix broke a case the agent itself identified as important. The agent's own test code stating 'Expected: False' confirms the agent recognized the correct behavior, making the 'Result: True' output an unambiguous failure of the fix, not a test-setup ambiguity.

CLOSE-LOOKING EXCLUSION: Distinguish between (a) a test failure caused by the fix being wrong (function returns a wrong value for a correctly set up test case — e.g., 'Result: True, Expected: False' for a lookup not in list_filter) and (b) a test failure caused by environment issues (ModuleNotFoundError, ImproperlyConfigured, RuntimeError about app_label, missing pytest). Type (a) is fix-breaking evidence; type (b) is environment noise that does not reflect fix quality. Also distinguish between a continuation that runs the full existing test suite (many 'ok' results across dozens of tests) and one that runs only a single existing test by name. The former is much stronger validation evidence. When a continuation shows both a regression in one step and a re-test that passes in a later step for seemingly the same lookup, the regression is still real evidence of a bug — the difference in results likely stems from different model definitions or list_filter configurations in the test setups, and the regression reveals the fix is too permissive under certain conditions. Do not dismiss the regression merely because a later re-test with a different setup passes.

MISLEADING PATTERN REJECTED: The pattern 'more passing custom tests = better fix' is misleading when one of those tests reveals a regression. The judge must not count test passes and regressions as equal-weight signals. A continuation that tests 8 cases and finds 1 regression has demonstrated its fix is broken, while a continuation that tests fewer custom cases, finds no regressions, and runs the full existing test suite has demonstrated its fix is correct. The judge conflated test quantity with fix correctness: the continuation with more passing custom tests also had a visible regression where lookup_allowed returned True for a blocked lookup, while the continuation with fewer custom tests had no regressions and a full existing test suite pass. A regression in a security function's core contract — allowing a lookup that should be blocked — is a veto-level signal that must override all positive test counts. A fix that is too permissive is fundamentally broken even if it fixes the reported bug, because it introduces a new security vulnerability.

ABSTENTION BOUNDARY: If no continuation shows a visible regression (all test outputs show Expected matching Result, or test outputs are truncated so Expected/Result are not visible), and no continuation runs the full existing test suite, do not distinguish based on custom test count alone. If the regression test output is truncated and the Expected/Result values are not visible, do not infer a regression from the agent's commentary or test name alone. If all continuations show only environment failures with no behavioral test results, the fix quality is unobservable from the visible evidence. This experience does not apply when the regression is in a non-security function where over-permissiveness does not violate a core contract — the veto-level weight is specific to security allowlist, permission, and validation-gate functions where allowing a blocked operation is a security vulnerability.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Security Regression: Over-Permissive lookup_allowed Allows Blocked Lookups
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluates whether the fix introduces a security regression where ModelAdmin.lookup_allowed() returns True (allows) for a lookup that should be blocked because it's not in list_filter. This is a veto-level flaw: the function's core security contract is to block unauthorized lookups, and a fix that allows a blocked lookup has introduced a vulnerability. Evidence includes visible test output showing 'Result: True' when 'Expected: False' for a lookup not in list_filter. This regression outweighs any number of passing custom tests because it demonstrates the fix is fundamentally broken - it fixes the reported bug but breaks the security gate. A continuation showing this regression must be ranked below one with no regressions that passes the full existing test suite.

scale.1: No evidence of over-permissiveness; all visible test outputs show lookup_allowed correctly blocks lookups not in list_filter (Result: False, Expected: False), or no security-relevant test outputs are visible
scale.2: Minor concern: fix passes main reproduction test but security-relevant edge cases are untested or test outputs are truncated so Expected/Result cannot be verified
scale.3: Moderate concern: agent identifies a potential over-permissiveness case in custom tests but the test setup is ambiguous (e.g., model definition unclear, list_filter configuration unclear), making it uncertain if it's a real regression
scale.4: Clear evidence of regression: visible test output shows 'Result: True' when 'Expected: False' for a lookup explicitly not in list_filter, with a clear model setup demonstrating the lookup should be blocked. The agent's own test code confirms the expected behavior.
scale.5: Most severe regression: clear over-permissiveness demonstrated in multiple test cases, or the fix allows all lookups through (e.g., returns True unconditionally), completely breaking the security contract. The continuation may have many passing custom tests but the regression is decisive.

metadata.judge_focus: Whether any visible test output shows lookup_allowed returning True for a lookup not in list_filter (Expected: False). Distinguish between (a) a real regression where the fix is too permissive (function returns wrong value for correctly set up test) and (b) environment failures (ModuleNotFoundError, ImproperlyConfigured). Also check if the continuation runs the full existing test suite (many 'ok' results) which is stronger validation than custom tests alone.
metadata.failure_mode: Fix passes the reported bug's reproduction test and many custom edge-case tests, but shows a visible regression where a blocked lookup is allowed. The agent may not recognize this as a security vulnerability and may continue adding more passing tests without addressing the regression.
metadata.oracle_test: Create a ModelAdmin with list_filter=['book__author'] and verify lookup_allowed('book__publisher', 'test_value') returns False. A correct fix must return False; an over-permissive fix returns True.

experiences.title: Inspectdb FK to Non-PK Field: Generated Constructor Syntax Beats Substring Success
experiences.description: Use this when judging continuations for the inspectdb foreign-key-to-specific-field task and the visible evidence includes generated model output, custom validation scripts, or final patch submissions. Rank by whether the generated model line is both semantically correct and valid Python/Django constructor syntax, not by submission status, a simple `to_field` substring check, or an agent's claim that edge cases pass.
experiences.context: This applies to the paused judge view for the task where inspectdb should generate a ForeignKey/OneToOneField pointing to a non-primary unique referenced column using `to_field`. The decisive visible evidence is the generated model text printed by the agent's own tests and inherited parent trajectory. A continuation that only proves the substring `to_field` appears can still be wrong if the output places a keyword argument before a later positional argument, producing invalid Python such as `models.ForeignKey('Foo', to_field='other_id', models.DO_NOTHING, ...)`. Evidence from a shared parent prefix remains relevant for descendant continuations unless a later visible diff or generated output clearly fixes it.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Retrieve this experience when a branch modifies inspectdb relationship generation and visible commands print generated model definitions or run scripts that assert `to_field` presence. It is especially important when multiple continuations share a parent patch and some submit after checking only whether `to_field` appears.

Decisive positive evidence: The generated relationship line includes `to_field='other_id'` or an equivalent referenced-column keyword while preserving valid constructor argument order. Examples of strong positive evidence visible in this round include output shaped like `models.ForeignKey('Foo', models.DO_NOTHING, to_field='other_id', blank=True, null=True)`, or any equivalent all-keyword form where no positional argument follows a keyword. A relevant edge-case script returning success can add confidence, but only after the actual generated model line is syntactically valid.

Decisive contradictory evidence: Output shaped like `models.ForeignKey('Foo', to_field='other_id', models.DO_NOTHING, blank=True, null=True)` is not a valid fix: it puts `to_field` before the later positional `models.DO_NOTHING`, which would make the generated model invalid Python. Do not credit a script that prints `SUCCESS: to_field is present` or `TEST PASSED` when its own printed model line has this invalid argument order. Also treat a custom script line such as `Test 2 FAILED: FK to unique field should have to_field` as contradictory even if the process return code is zero or the agent says all edge cases are working.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not require the field attribute name to be exactly `other_id`; inspectdb may validly emit a relation field named `other` for a database column named `other_id` if the resulting model maps correctly. Do not require a particular diff size, insertion count, or exact implementation shape. Do not penalize a branch merely for a failed attempt to run a broad test suite when other visible output directly shows the relevant generated model line is valid. Conversely, a submitted branch, a patch file display, or a passing substring assertion is not enough if the generated constructor syntax is visibly invalid.

Abstention boundary: If the visible prefix never shows the generated ForeignKey/OneToOneField line and the diff is too truncated to determine argument ordering, do not infer correctness or incorrectness from `to_field` mentions alone. Score uncertain branches in the middle unless there is inherited parent evidence showing the same unchanged patch produced valid or invalid model output.

Explicitly reject the misleading bias: Do not rank a continuation higher just because it submitted quickly, checked the basic reproduction, or printed a success message for `to_field` presence. The observed rubric focus on “submitted after only basic reproduction validation” is incomplete for this round: the more decisive discriminator is whether the generated model is valid Python with `models.DO_NOTHING`/`on_delete` placed legally relative to `to_field`. A branch with less polished finalization but valid generated constructor syntax should outrank a submitted branch whose own output shows invalid argument ordering.

experiences.title: Do Not Let Syntax-Only Verification Beat Targeted Changelist Transaction Validation
experiences.description: For paused Django admin changelist transaction tasks, reject rankings that favor a syntactically valid but behaviorally unvalidated, truncated edit over continuations that are actively validating or locating the relevant changelist/list_editable tests. A visible `ast.parse` success or an agent claim that an edit “looks good” is not decisive evidence that list_editable database mutations are correctly atomic.
experiences.context: Applies to the paused judge view for adding transaction handling to Django admin `changelist_view` list_editable processing. The visible continuations include mechanical edits to `django/contrib/admin/options.py`, backup restorations, truncated `sed`/`cat` inspections, failed imports due to missing dependencies, attempts to run admin changelist tests, dependency installation, and searches for `list_editable` or `changelist_view` tests.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions:
- Activate when the task is to add transaction handling to Django admin changelist/list_editable POST processing.
- Activate especially when the paused view is mid-trajectory, command output is truncated, and candidate continuations differ between: mechanical wrapper edits, syntax-only checks, backup restores, and targeted test discovery or execution.

Decisive positive evidence:
- The continuation visibly identifies the exact list_editable POST path in `changelist_view` and the data-changing save/logging operations that need atomic protection.
- The visible inspected code actually shows `transaction.atomic(...)` protecting the intended mutation block, using the appropriate write database routing when applicable, without corrupting surrounding formset/media construction.
- The continuation makes targeted validation progress: running or attempting to run admin changelist/list_editable tests, installing missing dependencies as part of that attempt, resolving settings/test-runner issues, or searching for the exact existing tests that exercise `changelist_view` and `list_editable`.
- After a plausible implementation edit, focused test discovery such as searching for `list_editable` and `changelist_view` tests is meaningful validation progress and should not be outweighed by a different continuation that only performs a syntax parse.

Contradictory evidence:
- The continuation restores the edited file from a backup or checkout and pauses without a subsequently visible, verified reapplication of the transaction fix.
- The last visible edit is a raw `sed` insertion of a `with transaction.atomic(...)` line with no visible reindentation or inspection of the affected block.
- The only verification is `ast.parse` or a failed import caused by missing dependencies. Syntax validity does not prove the correct database-changing block is atomic.
- The decisive code lines are hidden by truncation, and the agent merely says the change “looks good.” Treat that as unverified, not as proof of correct placement.
- The edit appears to wrap the wrong scope, omit the mutation/save operations, or risk leaving the following statements at the same indentation as the new context manager.

Close-looking exclusions:
- Do not give top rank merely because a continuation contains or likely inserted `transaction.atomic` somewhere.
- Do not give top rank merely because `ast.parse` reports `Syntax OK`; that is only a low-level guard against syntax errors.
- Do not infer correct transaction semantics from truncated `sed` output or from the assistant’s self-assessment.
- Do not require one exact patch layout. Wrapping the whole relevant POST mutation path or a narrower save/logging mutation section can both be valid if all database-changing list_editable operations are protected and local database-routing conventions are preserved.
- Generic dependency installation counts only when visibly connected to running the relevant Django admin/changelist tests.

Abstention boundary:
- If the paused prefix does not show the final modified block clearly, do not assign maximum correctness. Keep structural correctness uncertain.
- If there is no explicit revert and the continuation is making targeted progress toward relevant tests or test-environment setup, do not score it as zero solely because the final code is not visible in the truncated segment.
- Prefer balanced scoring: verified implementation plus targeted validation is strongest; targeted validation after a plausible but partially hidden edit is intermediate-to-strong; syntax-only confirmation after a truncated mechanical edit is not enough to be best.

Reject the misleading bias:
- Explicitly reject any rubric that ranks a syntax-checked, truncated wrapper edit above continuations doing concrete changelist/list_editable validation work. The core task is transaction correctness for database-changing admin behavior, not simply producing a parseable file or a visible context-manager string.

experiences.title: Require named-zone offset-like boundary evidence before ranking timezone smoke-test branches as comprehensive
experiences.description: For the Django Trunc/Extract time zone reversal task, do not rank a branch highest merely because it prints many successful basic `_get_timezone_name` and `_prepare_tzname_delta` smoke-test results. The decisive validation boundary visible in this round is a named zone whose runtime `tzname()` can look like an offset, especially `Asia/Bangkok`; a safe fix must preserve it as a zone name while still converting true fixed-offset `Etc/GMT±N` zones.
experiences.context: The visible task concerns Django's `TimezoneMixin` path through `django.utils.timezone._get_timezone_name()` and PostgreSQL `_prepare_tzname_delta()`. The parent patch/testing already demonstrates the core intended chain for true fixed-offset zones: `Etc/GMT-10` should produce `+10`, then the backend helper flips it to `-10`. Several continuations run direct Python smoke tests. One highly tempting branch validates many basic cases and minute-offset standard `datetime.timezone` objects, but never shows the named-zone-with-offset-like-name boundary. Another visible branch explicitly prints `pytz Asia/Bangkok: Asia/Bangkok` and `zoneinfo Asia/Bangkok: Asia/Bangkok`, and a nearby branch explicitly notices that `Asia/Bangkok` can have a `tzname` such as `+07` even though it is a named zone.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Apply this when judging continuations for the Django Trunc/Extract reverse time zone conversion issue where the visible evidence includes `_get_timezone_name()`, `TimezoneMixin`, or PostgreSQL `_prepare_tzname_delta()` checks, and candidate branches are mostly validating a source change with `python -c` smoke tests. It is especially activated when one branch shows many successful outputs for `Etc/GMT-10`, `Etc/GMT+10`, `UTC`, `US/Eastern`, `Europe/London`, standard fixed offsets, or minute offsets, while another branch shows or discusses `Asia/Bangkok` as a named zone whose `tzname()` can look like `+07`.

Decisive positive evidence: Prefer a branch that visibly proves the fix does not overgeneralize offset-looking `tzname()` values from named zones. Strong visible proof includes output such as `_get_timezone_name(pytz.timezone('Asia/Bangkok')) == 'Asia/Bangkok'` and `_get_timezone_name(ZoneInfo('Asia/Bangkok')) == 'Asia/Bangkok'`, or source evidence of an implementation that only uses the offset name for true fixed-offset/Etc zones and falls back to the zone key/string for named zones. This evidence should be ranked above broader-looking smoke tests that omit the named-zone boundary. It is also positive when the trajectory explicitly recognizes the mechanism: `Asia/Bangkok` may report `+07` as a runtime abbreviation/offset, but it must remain a named zone for this Django API.

Contradictory evidence: A branch is not comprehensive merely because it prints correct results for `pytz` and `zoneinfo` `Etc/GMT-10`, `Etc/GMT+10`, `UTC`, `US/Eastern`, `Europe/London`, `Etc/GMT-5`, standard `datetime.timezone(+10/-10)`, or minute-offset standard timezones such as `+0530` and `-0330`. Those outputs validate the obvious fixed-offset path but do not rule out the dangerous overbroad implementation that converts any offset-looking `tzname(datetime)` into a SQL offset. Similarly, a full-chain printout `_get_timezone_name=+10` then `_prepare_tzname_delta=-10` for `Etc/GMT-10` is necessary but not sufficient to outrank explicit `Asia/Bangkok` preservation evidence.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not treat minute-precision standard offsets as a substitute for `Asia/Bangkok`; they test a different boundary. Do not treat `US/Eastern` or `Europe/London` as sufficient named-zone guards, because their visible names do not exercise the offset-like `tzname` trap. Do not give extra credit for an initial failed `django.setup()` or a failed/misaddressed test-runner command; only the subsequent successful smoke output matters. Conversely, do not require one exact implementation pattern: a valid fix may use `tzname(None)` with fallback, inspect a stable zone key/string, or otherwise distinguish true fixed-offset zones from named zones, as long as it preserves named-zone semantics and produces the required fixed-offset output.

Explicit rejection of the misleading scoring bias: Reject any rubric or judge preference that treats volume of successful direct Python smoke tests, PostgreSQL helper-chain output, or minute-offset standard-timezone checks as “comprehensive” validation when the named-zone offset-like boundary is absent. In this round, a branch without visible `Asia/Bangkok` preservation or clearly safe source-code discrimination should not be ranked above a branch that visibly preserves `Asia/Bangkok` for both `pytz` and `zoneinfo`.

Abstention boundary: If no visible branch shows `Asia/Bangkok` or another named zone with offset-like `tzname()` behavior, and the source code discriminator is too truncated to determine whether named zones are preserved, then do not infer correctness or incorrectness from basic `Etc/GMT` smoke tests alone. Rank using other observable evidence, but do not label the validation comprehensive. If the full source change is visible and clearly preserves named zones by construction, explicit `Asia/Bangkok` output is helpful but not mandatory.

experiences.title: Second manual correction: Priority visible-state rule: Inner-class makemigrations judging: prefer exact migration-writer test engagement, reject FunctionTypeSerializer detours
experiences.description:
SECOND-PASS MANDATORY RULE: A real official migration-writer failure and expected qualified-path inspection must dominate self-written green checks.

Positive visible evidence: Executed official test, real failure, and expected qualified path.
Contradictory or insufficient visible evidence: Self-written serializer or makemigrations success and unrelated completeness criteria.

MANDATORY RULE: A legacy overfit card changed tie-aware selection using evidence already present in this exact visible trajectory. Its text is retained only as a starting point and must pass the standard recall@6 gate again.

Background: For the Django makemigrations inner-class path task, do not rank a continuation highest merely because custom self-authored scripts print success or because it broadens the fix to FunctionTypeSerializer. The decisive visible evidence is engagement with the actual migration writer/type serialization contract for inner classes: TypeSerializer or field deconstruction using the full qualified class name, actual makemigrations output containing Outer.Inner or Thing.State, and especially running the existing migration writer test target and inspecting its expectations.
experiences.context: The paused view concerns Django migration serialization for inner classes. The reported bug is that a field subclass or enum class defined inside another class is emitted as module.Inner or module.State instead of module.Outer.Inner or module.Thing.State. The parent trajectory already shows the core source area: django/db/migrations/serializer.py TypeSerializer using self.value.__qualname__. The continuations mostly differ in validation and follow-up investigation: some run custom scripts that pass, one invokes the project test runner after installing the project and runs migrations.test_writer.WriterTests.test_deconstruct_class_arguments with a real failure, some try nonexistent test_serializer targets, and one later changes FunctionTypeSerializer based on a broad grep for __name__.
experiences.experience:
Second manual correction after inspecting the failed generated rubric and evidence-first scores:
A real official migration-writer failure and expected qualified-path inspection must dominate self-written green checks.

Credit only this visible evidence: Executed official test, real failure, and expected qualified path.
Reject or cap this visible evidence: Self-written serializer or makemigrations success and unrelated completeness criteria.
Abstain when: Without an executed official oracle, assign diagnosis credit only.

Do not let another retrieved experience replace this task-specific rule with a generic process proxy.

Priority override for rubric generation and weighting:
A legacy overfit card changed tie-aware selection using evidence already present in this exact visible trajectory. Its text is retained only as a starting point and must pass the standard recall@6 gate again.

Reject any generated rubric whose direction, anchors, or weighting contradicts that rule. Apply it only to the matching visible task and stage; otherwise abstain.

Activation: Use this experience when judging this paused round for the Django inner-class makemigrations issue, especially when comparing continuations that already appear to have the TypeSerializer/__qualname__ change and differ mainly by validation commands, custom tests, and possible extra edits around FunctionTypeSerializer.

Core task boundary: The visible user issue is about migration paths for classes used as field classes or class-valued field arguments: Outer.Inner and Thing.State must appear in generated migration code. A minimal TypeSerializer or deconstruction-path change that preserves the full qualified class name is a valid implementation. Do not require a broad sweep of every __name__ occurrence, and do not require a FunctionTypeSerializer/classmethod change to consider the inner-field makemigrations bug addressed.

Decisive positive evidence: A continuation that installs the project into the Python environment and then invokes the actual project test runner on migrations.test_writer.WriterTests.test_deconstruct_class_arguments is showing the strongest visible validation/investigation signal in this paused view. The output with F, Ran 1 test, FAILED (failures=1), Testing against Django installed in '/testbed/django', and System check identified no issues is a real project test result, not a setup failure. If the continuation then greps the test source for test_deconstruct_class_arguments, that is additional positive evidence that it is comparing the fix against existing migration-writer expectations. This should outrank a continuation that only shows custom self-authored scripts printing ALL TESTS PASSED.

Other positive evidence: Direct serializer checks such as serializer_factory(Outer.Inner) returning __main__.Outer.Inner, serializer_factory(Thing.State) returning __main__.Thing.State, field deconstruct paths containing Outer.Inner, and actual makemigrations output containing test_app.models.Outer.Inner or enum=test_app.models.Thing.State are relevant and should receive credit. Checks preserving built-in special cases such as str, int, type(None), and models.Model are also useful compatibility evidence. These custom checks are valid supporting evidence, but in this paused comparison they are less discriminative than real project migration-writer test engagement.

Contradictory evidence: Do not credit commands that merely look like test activity but fail to load or target nonexistent tests: No module named pytest, no tests/migrations/test_serializer.py, unittest.loader._FailedTest, ModuleNotFoundError, ImproperlyConfigured, Ran 0 tests, TypeError from a bad test invocation, or output that contains a traceback even if the shell return code is 0 because the command was piped through head. Also do not treat a self-authored test script’s ALL TESTS PASSED banner as decisive when the same continuation has not exercised the project migration-writer tests.

Contradictory evidence for overbroad fixes: A later sed edit replacing klass.__name__ with klass.__qualname__ in FunctionTypeSerializer is not decisive positive evidence for this task. FunctionTypeSerializer is about function or bound-method serialization, while the visible bug report concerns inner classes used in makemigrations for fields and enum class arguments. If the continuation does not visibly validate the bound-method change afterward, the extra edit should not lift it above a continuation with stronger migration-writer validation. Likewise, a branch that claims DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path is another issue based only on synthetic __main__.Outer imports is following a detour unless it shows an actual migration output problem for the reported case.

Close-looking exclusions: Distinguish a real failure in migrations.test_writer.WriterTests.test_deconstruct_class_arguments from setup failures. The former ran one named project test and produced a normal unittest failure result; the latter show import/configuration errors or failed test discovery and do not validate anything. Distinguish nonexistent migrations.test_serializer targets from the visible existing tests in tests/migrations/test_writer.py. Distinguish built-in type serialization expectations: visible outputs show builtins may serialize as str or int rather than builtins.str, so a custom script initially expecting builtins.int and then correcting it is not evidence against the TypeSerializer fix. Distinguish the core TypeSerializer class-path behavior from FunctionTypeSerializer bound-method behavior; do not penalize an otherwise correct minimal inner-class fix for not touching FunctionTypeSerializer.

Abstention boundary: If the paused view lacks visible source evidence of the TypeSerializer/deconstruction path and lacks visible serializer, makemigrations, or project test output, abstain from distinguishing branch quality. If two continuations both show the same core qualified-path behavior and comparably relevant validation, preserve them as equivalent rather than preferring the one with more custom printouts. If project test output is fully truncated so that the test name and whether it is a real failure versus a setup failure cannot be seen, do not infer its significance.

Misleading rubric or judge-bias rejection: Explicitly reject any scoring criterion that expands this task into “fix every inner-class serialization path” or requires a FunctionTypeSerializer/classmethod edit as a completeness condition. Also reject the bias that custom ALL TESTS PASSED output is stronger than a real project migration-writer test result that fails on a relevant assertion. The ranking must follow the visible task contract: correct qualified paths for inner classes in makemigrations, with validation weighted by relevance to Django’s migration writer rather than by superficial pass banners or broad grep-based extra edits.

Positive visible evidence: Executed official test, real failure, and expected qualified path. Contradictory or insufficient visible evidence: Self-written serializer or makemigrations success and unrelated completeness criteria.

experiences.title: Django aggregate-over-window: failed post-fix validation overrides correct-looking get_aggregation Ref/subquery edits
experiences.description: For this Django ORM round, do not reward a continuation as strong simply because it edits or discusses get_aggregation, Ref replacement, or preserving window annotations. If the same branch then runs the issue reproduction and still gets `OperationalError: misuse of window function SUM()`, that visible failed validation is decisive evidence the fix does not work.
experiences.context: The paused view concerns Django 4.2 failing on `queryset.annotate(cumul_DJR=Coalesce(Window(Sum("DJR"), order_by=F("date").asc()), 0.0)).aggregate(DJR_total=Sum("DJR"), cumul_DJR_total=Sum("cumul_DJR"))`. The desired behavior is a two-level query shape: compute the window annotation in an inner query and aggregate its alias in an outer query, producing the sample totals `DJR_total = 600.0` and `cumul_DJR_total = 1000.0`. The misleading branch in the paused view has comments such as keeping `Ref`s to annotations containing window functions in `django/db/models/sql/query.py`, even inserts a debug print, but its own later validation still prints `Error: OperationalError misuse of window function SUM()` for the SUM-over-window test.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Apply this experience when judging trajectories for the visible Django aggregate-over-window issue and the branch is working around `get_aggregation`, `Ref(...)`, annotation masks, subquery selection, or the decision of whether aggregation must use a subquery.

Decisive positive evidence: Strong progress is visible when a continuation identifies that the problem is not merely how the subquery branch rewrites `Ref`s, but that the normal/non-subquery path may still be selected even though an aggregate references an annotation whose expression has `contains_over_clause=True`. Especially strong evidence includes: observing `cumul_DJR_total` references `cumul_DJR`; detecting that the referenced annotation contains a window clause; adding or planning a condition that forces/materializes an inner query for such references; showing SQL where the inner query selects `COALESCE(SUM(...) OVER (...)) AS cumul_DJR` and the outer query aggregates that alias; or validating the sample result as `(600.0, 1000.0)`.

Decisive contradictory evidence: If a continuation applies a purported fix and then runs the issue reproduction with visible output still showing `OperationalError misuse of window function SUM()`, treat the fix as disproven. This is true even if the changed code is in `django/db/models/sql/query.py`, mentions `Ref`, detects `contains_over_clause`, or appears to preserve window annotations. A post-fix result of `cumul_DJR_total: 0.0` for the three-row sample is also contradictory because the expected cumulative sum total is `1000.0`, not zero.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not give high credit merely for a comment like “First, check for Refs to annotations containing window functions,” for a script printing “Fix is in the file,” for inspecting `Ref.replace_expressions`, or for editing only the already-subquery branch around the inner-query replacement loop. Those can look like the correct layer but still fail if the query never enters the subquery path. A manual raw-SQL subquery demonstration is useful diagnostic evidence, but it is not by itself an implemented ORM fix. Finding `refs_subquery` or `has_existing_aggregation` is partial progress only unless the continuation connects it to aggregate references to window annotations.

Misleading rubric or judge-bias rejection: Reject any scoring bias that treats matching the static pattern “get_aggregation + Ref replacement + keep window annotations” as decisive. In this round, visible execution results are stronger than the code-pattern match. A branch with an apparently relevant `query.py` edit must rank below branches still productively isolating the actual subquery-decision failure if its own validation shows the original database error remains.

Equivalent valid implementations: Preserve credit for any implementation that prevents generating `SUM(window_function)` at the same SQL level and instead aggregates over a materialized/aliased window result, even if it does not use the exact variable names or code location suggested above. The key semantic requirement is to avoid nesting the aggregate directly around the window expression while preserving ordinary aggregates such as `Sum("DJR")`.

Abstention boundary: If a branch has not run validation after its latest patch, or the visible output is truncated before the relevant result/error, do not assume the patch fails. Score it on static evidence and stated reasoning. Only treat the fix as disproven when the visible post-fix run shows the original `misuse of window function SUM()` error or an explicitly wrong aggregate total for the sample case.

experiences.title: SQLite Decimal Window Branch Ranking: Prefer Current Outer-CAST Patch plus Completed Official OK, Not Truncated or Invalid Custom Validation
experiences.description: Use when judging paused trajectories for the SQLite Lag/Window DecimalField crash whose visible bad SQL is `CAST(LAG(...) AS NUMERIC) OVER (...)`. The ranking must prioritize visible current correctness: a current Window-level fix that produces `CAST(LAG(...) OVER (...) AS NUMERIC)` and completed official test output. Do not let broad-looking but truncated test runs, custom `All tests passed!` messages, or invalid exploratory Window API scripts outweigh visible SQL placement and current diff evidence.
experiences.context: Activation: Apply to this round’s Django SQLite DecimalField window-function issue after the prompt shows the original syntax error and generated SQL with `CAST` ending before `OVER`. The paused view includes branch summaries, parent-state evidence, current diffs or diff snippets, generated SQL from custom scripts, and official test runner output. Parent evidence can support a continuation only if the continuation still shows the same current patch and no later current-diff contradiction. Current branch evidence overrides inherited claims when it shows checkout/no diff, wrong-class edits, missing casts, or runtime errors from the patch.
experiences.experience:
Decisive positive evidence: Rank a branch highly when the visible current state shows a localized fix in the Window compilation path, or an equivalent narrowly scoped mechanism, and either the reproduction SQL or tests confirm the DecimalField window expression is compiled as a single outer numeric cast: `CAST(LAG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) AS NUMERIC) AS "w"`. A completed official test run with visible `Ran ...` and `OK` is strong supporting evidence, especially when paired with the same current patch summary inherited from a parent that already reached `expressions_window` OK. Broad official suites that visibly end with `OK` should count more than custom script banners.

Contradictory evidence: Penalize branches whose current state has no code change after a checkout, an empty current diff, or visible Window-specific `source_expression`/`window_sql` logic placed inside `SQLiteNumericMixin` where it can run for `Lag` and raise `AttributeError: 'Lag' object has no attribute 'source_expression'`. Also penalize custom output for the DecimalField reproduction that prints `LAG(...) OVER (...) AS "w"` with no surrounding `CAST(... AS NUMERIC)`, even if it also prints `SUCCESS!` or `All tests passed!`. Treat official test output that is truncated to migrations, setup, or `System check identified no issues` without visible `Ran`/`OK` as inconclusive, not as a suite pass. Pytest collection/settings/app-registry errors are not validation.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not demote an otherwise correct current patch because later exploratory scripts tried expressions that the Window API visibly rejects, such as `Coalesce`, `F`, or `CombinedExpression` directly in `Window`, or a `WindowFrame(rows=...)` constructor shape that raises a type error. Those are invalid custom tests, not regressions of the DecimalField outer-CAST fix. Conversely, do not elevate a branch because it ran many custom edge-case scripts, added many lines, or printed a success banner when the visible SQL lacks the DecimalField cast or the official test completion is not visible. Regression checks for FloatField or explicit `output_field=FloatField()` are useful only after the default DecimalField outer-CAST contract is satisfied; they must not outrank the primary contract.

Preserve equivalent valid implementations: Do not require one exact spelling such as a direct `source_expression.as_sql()` call if the visible implementation and generated SQL demonstrate that the inner window function avoids the premature SQLite numeric cast and the completed window expression receives a single DecimalField-only outer cast. A small Window-level method, a helper, or another localized compilation path can be valid. What is not equivalent is moving Window assembly into the generic SQLite numeric mixin for all functions, dropping the DecimalField cast entirely, or relying on validation breadth while the current SQL/diff contradicts the outer-CAST contract.

Abstention boundary: If no current diff, no decisive generated SQL, and no completed `Ran ... OK` output are visible, do not rank a branch at the top based on patch size, return code, or test-script quantity. Give only partial credit for a single custom reproduction success without visible current diff or official completion, because unseen current-code regressions remain possible. Explicitly reject the misleading judging bias that treats return code 0, truncated test tails, or `All tests passed!` banners as stronger than visible SQL placement and current patch evidence.

experiences.title: Error-message contract over regression-test proxy
experiences.description: Use when a framework validation task asks to enrich an existing diagnostic message with the offending option value, and the trajectory has localized the message formatter and shown the value is already available.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django-like framework codebase during implementation or final review of an admin/system-check diagnostic change, especially when the task explicitly says an indexed option error such as readonly_fields[0] omits the bad field name while comparable option checks include it. The criterion is useful once the trajectory has found the relevant item-level validation path, identified the indexed label and offending value variables, or reproduced/computed the message. It is less useful for early exploration before the error site is known, for tasks that require changing validation semantics rather than only message content, or when the only visible issue is missing test-suite integration and the behavior contract is already unquestionably satisfied.
experiences.experience:
The strongest rubric in these cases judges the actual diagnostic contract: invalid readonly_fields entries must report both the indexed option label and the offending field name/value, without changing what counts as valid. This aligns because the decisive visible evidence is whether the agent located the existing readonly_fields error construction, recognized that the label only contains readonly_fields[index], compared nearby checks that say the option “refers to” a field value, and planned or applied a localized message interpolation using the existing field value.

Rubrics that make a project-native regression test mandatory are weaker here: tests are desirable, but the core task acceptance is the emitted admin.E035-style message content and unchanged validation behavior. A better rubric should focus on preserving the existing error id, indexed label, admin/model context, and accepted cases such as callables, admin attributes, model attributes, and real model fields.

When scoring edge cases, map polarity to the framework’s existing validation predicate rather than inventing a stricter rule. If the task is only to improve the message, then equivalent implementations that keep the same valid/invalid boundary should be rewarded, and rubrics should not demand rejection of cases the current contract accepts. The negative criterion is changing validation semantics, error identity, or context while adding the value; the positive criterion is a localized message-content change that preserves those semantics.

Avoid tempting proxies such as requiring a helper refactor, requiring exact test-run success in a difficult local framework test environment, requiring broad changes to admin checks, or adding unrelated validation-condition requirements. Prioritize visible evidence from code inspection, manual reproduction output, targeted tests, or patch intent showing the offending value appears in the invalid-readonly-field message while the validation branches remain intact. Preserve uncertainty when the visible trajectory has not exposed the relevant edge-case behavior; do not penalize or reward speculative semantic changes without evidence.

experiences.title: Do not use methodical debugging, patch presence, fix abstraction level, or diagnosis accuracy as proxies for root-cause-to-fix alignment
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when an agent is tracing a complex framework bug step-by-step, but the key evaluation question is whether the agent's stated root cause matches the visible failure mode and whether any implemented patch directly addresses that root cause and produces the expected behavior — not whether the debugging process is orderly, whether a patch exists, whether the fix is at a presumed-correct 'general' abstraction level, or whether the diagnosis alone is accurate. Fix correctness must be evaluated independently from root-cause identification: a correct diagnosis with an incorrect fix must score strictly lower than correct diagnosis plus a working fix.
experiences.context: Applies in Python framework/library bug fixes such as Django ORM, Matplotlib axes/autoscale, or SymPy polynomial internals where the trajectory shows reproduction, code inspection, tracing, and one-at-a-time hypotheses, but the candidate direction may still target an intermediate symptom instead of the contract-breaking boundary. The source rubric may still be appropriate early in an investigation when the main visible risk is shotgun-editing many unrelated areas without isolating failures. It is misleading as a final-review or late-debugging criterion when the agent has already narrowed to a plausible subsystem and correctness depends on preserving a specific behavior: per-parent slicing semantics, shared-axis unit propagation, queryset immutability/select-list invariants, lazy related-object normalization, or algebraic factor preservation. Also applies when a task requires both root-cause diagnosis and a code fix and the issue describes a feature that works in one code path but fails in another — in these cases diagnosis quality must not inflate fix-correctness scores. Abstain when the prefix does not contain enough evidence to determine whether the agent's root cause analysis is correct, or when no branch has both a stated root cause and a patch to compare alignment, or when the visible prefix shows only exploration with no applied patches or test results and cannot distinguish whether a continuation's fix would work.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged whether the agent tested hypotheses one at a time and avoided shotgun debugging. That is useful process guidance, but in these cases it often over-rewarded trajectories that were orderly yet still wrong: the agent traced a real symptom, then patched a nearby mechanism without proving that the patch satisfied the user-visible invariant. A better rubric should focus on validated root-cause-to-fix alignment, evaluated as two independent dimensions: (1) whether the agent identified the exact root-cause mechanism matching the visible failure, and (2) whether the implemented fix produces the expected behavior described in the issue. Do not collapse these into a single ascending scale where correct diagnosis earns near-maximum scores — a continuation that correctly identifies the root cause but implements a fix that does not resolve the issue must score in the lower half, strictly below one that both diagnoses and fixes correctly.
