reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that deleting a legacy composite index targets only the non-unique index when uniqueness-bearing constraints exist on the same columns. Strong evidence includes identifying the schema editor composed-index deletion path, explaining that unique constraints may also be reported as indexes by introspection, applying or proposing a filter equivalent to index=True and unique=False for ordinary index deletion, and checking that the uniqueness declaration remains intact. Full-credit evidence must show comprehensive exclusion of unique colliders, not merely exclusion of a primary-key subtype or reliance on generated name patterns.

metadata.primary_failure_mode: constraint lookup for ordinary index deletion matches both unique and non-unique database objects on the same columns
metadata.decisive_observable_distinction: broad non-unique-index predicate versus subtype-only filtering such as primary_key=False
key_positive_evidence: inspects schema editor composed-index deletion or equivalent migration database operation path
recognizes unique constraints can have index metadata in introspection
narrows ordinary index deletion to non-unique constraints/indexes using unique=False or an equivalent backend-correct predicate
preserves unique_together, UniqueConstraint, field-level unique, and primary-key uniqueness semantics where applicable
validates that removing the ordinary index leaves the uniqueness object intact
avoid_as_primary_evidence: relying only on generated constraint name suffixes
excluding only primary-key constraints while leaving other unique colliders eligible to match
generic migration autodetector changes without schema deletion disambiguation
validation unrelated to the duplicate constraint lookup behavior
treating declaration move/recreation optimization as required for the crash fix

scale.1: 1: No evidence that the trajectory distinguishes ordinary composite index deletion from uniqueness-bearing constraint deletion; it may only inspect files, run unrelated validation, or discuss migrations generically.
scale.2: 2: Weak evidence: the trajectory locates relevant schema or migration code and mentions duplicate constraints, but does not identify that unique constraints can also match an index lookup or proposes only a subtype-specific exclusion such as primary_key=False.
scale.3: 3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory understands that the same columns have both unique and non-unique database objects and considers filtering by constraint type, but the implementation or validation is incomplete or could still affect unique constraint deletion.
scale.4: 4: Strong evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly plans a fix that excludes unique constraints when deleting ordinary composite indexes and checks at least one focused reproduction or equivalent introspection path.
scale.5: 5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory directly targets the index_together deletion lookup with a non-unique index predicate, explains the introspection reason, verifies that the ordinary index is removed while the uniqueness object remains, and confirms related composed-index deletion semantics are not regressed.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Subtype-Only or Name-Based Filtering Leaves Ambiguous Matches
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that claim to fix the duplicate-match crash while leaving the ordinary index deletion lookup broad enough to match other unique objects. This includes edits that only add primary_key=False, only handle a primary-key collision in validation, or rely on suffix/name conventions instead of constraint semantics. The negative signal is strongest when visible evidence shows the lookup still lacks unique=False or an equivalent non-unique-index discriminator; preserve uncertainty if the relevant filtering or validation scope cannot be seen.

metadata.primary_failure_mode: implementation disambiguates one special unique subtype but not all uniqueness-bearing objects that can satisfy the lookup
key_negative_evidence: adds only primary_key=False to constraint filtering for an ordinary index deletion path
validates only a primary-key collision while claiming complete same-column disambiguation
does not address field-level unique=True, unique_together, UniqueConstraint, or equivalent unique colliders when they remain eligible under the lookup
uses generated constraint names or suffixes as the main discriminator
changes unrelated migration declaration logic without isolating the database object to delete
metadata.uncertainty_handling: If the visible material is truncated or the backend-specific equivalent predicate cannot be determined, avoid assuming either a comprehensive fix or a narrow subtype-only fix.

scale.1: 1: No evidence of subtype-only or name-based disambiguation; the trajectory either uses a semantic non-unique predicate or the relevant edit is not visible.
scale.2: 2: Minor concern: the trajectory mentions a special collider such as a primary key, but also appears to understand that unique constraints broadly must be excluded.
scale.3: 3: Moderate concern: the trajectory proposes a partial discriminator or narrow validation, and it is unclear whether other unique colliders would still match.
scale.4: 4: Strong concern: the visible edit or plan excludes only primary-key constraints, relies on names, or otherwise leaves field-level/declared unique constraints eligible to match the ordinary index lookup.
scale.5: 5: Severe concern: the trajectory explicitly treats primary-key-only exclusion or name matching as a complete fix despite evidence that other uniqueness-bearing objects share the lookup columns and flags.

experiences.title: Contract-Level Behavioral Test Evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an agent claims validation through added tests, changed expected outputs, or ad hoc scripts for a behavior-specific bug or feature; judge whether those tests assert the actual user-visible contract — including the exact set of produced values when the fix changes what is yielded or returned, and the exact per-branch or per-mode value/position assignments when the fix controls which specific values are selected per condition — rather than merely exercising code paths, confirming aggregate statistics match, or matching per-branch counts without verifying which specific values are assigned to each branch.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent trajectories across Python, Go, and TypeScript repositories after the agent has identified a fix and is using tests or manual scripts as confidence evidence. It is most relevant for tasks involving parsing metadata, fallback ordering, event-driven UI updates, set/membership semantics, deterministic selection, API parameter precedence, per-branch or per-mode value selection, or yield/return logic where a patch can look plausible while missing a boundary condition. It is less decisive during early exploration, when no implementation exists yet, or for very small localized source fixes whose correctness is directly visible from the changed line and no durable test has been added. Do not retrieve it merely because no formal test was run; absence of tests alone is not a reliable flaw for simple one-line compatibility fixes. Do retrieve it when tests are present but may be superficial, omitted from the submitted diff, only check that code runs, update expectations to match an incorrect intermediate representation, rely on aggregate statistics (e.g., matching copied/processed counts) that can be satisfied by wrong fixes which skip or duplicate items, or match per-branch counts without verifying which specific values or positions are assigned to each branch. Abstain from the aggregate-statistics criterion when the fix does not modify what is produced (yielded, returned, emitted output), or when the exact output cannot be observed from the visible prefix and only aggregate statistics are available.
experiences.experience: The prior rubric judged whether validation was meaningful. It was useful when visible test activity revealed whether the agent understood the behavioral contract: strong evidence came from tests that exercised the exact reported scenario, asserted the final observable result, and included important branches such as missing data, fallback paths, resize/update events, explicit override versus default behavior, or deterministic ordering. It correctly flagged trajectories where the agent relied on smoke scripts, repeated commands, changed expected values without checking the real semantic object, or added tests that did not cover the required fallback/edge case. However, it can be misleading if used as a blanket requirement: a tiny, obvious formatting or parameter-default fix may be correct even with weak or no committed tests. A better retrieved rubric should focus on the quality and relevance of the validation evidence, not on the mere presence, count, or passing status of tests. Avoid the tempting criterion 'tests pass, therefore patch is good' or 'no tests, therefore patch is bad.' Prioritize visible evidence that tests would fail on the original bug, assert the user-facing contract exactly, cover the boundary cases named in the task, and are actually part of the patch or otherwise reproducible from the trajectory. When a fix modifies what is produced (yielded, returned, emitted output), matching aggregate statistics — such as 'N files copied, N post-processed' or 'N items returned' — can be a false proxy: a wrong fix that skips or omits items can still produce matching counts. The discriminating evidence is whether each expected item appears exactly once in the output with its correct final value, not whether aggregate counts match. Prefer evidence that enumerates the exact output set (e.g., listing each yielded item with its final value) over evidence that only checks aggregate counts or command success. This distinction is critical because wrong fixes that eliminate duplicates by skipping yields, or that omit failing items, can produce the same aggregate counts as correct fixes that process each item exactly once. A parallel trap arises when a fix controls which specific values or positions are selected per branch, mode, or condition: per-branch count matching is still a false proxy. A fix can produce the correct count for each branch yet assign the wrong specific values to each branch — for example, reversing which boundary is included for one mode versus another. A symmetric case such as 'both' or 'all' can mask this reversal because it includes all values regardless of which direction the selection logic is reversed. The discriminating evidence is whether each branch's actual value or position assignments are verified independently, not inferred from per-branch counts or from a symmetric case that happens to work.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Meaningful Contract Validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the agent's validation evidence demonstrates the intended behavioral contract, not just code execution or aggregate statistics. High-quality evidence includes committed or clearly described tests/manual checks that reproduce the reported issue, assert the exact user-visible expected result, cover named edge cases and fallback/update paths, and would distinguish the proposed fix from common wrong implementations. When the fix modifies what is produced (yielded, returned, emitted output), the evidence should enumerate the exact output set — each item appearing exactly once with its correct final value — rather than relying on aggregate counts that can be satisfied by wrong fixes which skip or duplicate items. When the fix controls which specific values or positions are selected per branch or mode, the evidence should verify the actual per-branch value/position assignments independently — not just per-branch counts, and not via a symmetric case (e.g., 'both'/'all') that can mask asymmetric reversal errors where the correct count appears at wrong positions. This rubric should be applied relative to the current trajectory: look only at visible task requirements, test diffs, commands run, outputs observed, and whether validation artifacts are included or durable.

prioritize evidence: tests or scripts reproduce the specific reported behavior
assertions check exact semantic outputs or state changes, not merely absence of crashes
when the fix changes what is produced, assertions enumerate the exact output set — each item appears exactly once with its correct final value — not just matching aggregate counts

when the fix selects which specific values/positions are included per branch or mode, assertions verify the actual per-branch value/position assignments independently — not just per-branch counts, and not via a symmetric case that can mask asymmetric reversal errors

coverage includes task-specified boundaries such as fallback order, missing data, update events, deterministic selection, membership semantics, per-branch/per-mode value selection, or explicit override behavior
validation artifacts are committed or clearly part of the final patch when appropriate
test output confirms the relevant tests actually ran rather than being skipped or unmatched
deprioritize evidence: test count or broad suite pass status without relevant assertions
aggregate statistics (e.g., matching copied/processed counts) that can be satisfied by wrong fixes which skip or duplicate items, when the fix changes what is produced
per-branch counts that match expected values without verifying which specific values/positions are assigned to each branch
symmetric cases (e.g., 'both'/'all') used to infer correctness of asymmetric branches, when the symmetric case can mask reversal errors
manual scripts that only print values or check a superficial substring
updated expected values that mirror the implementation without checking the requested behavior
absence of tests for a trivial source-level fix whose correctness is directly inspectable
metadata.applicability stage: post-implementation or final-review stage, especially when the agent cites validation as confidence
metadata.abstain when: the fix does not modify what is produced (yielded, returned, output), or the exact output cannot be observed from the visible prefix and only aggregate statistics are available

scale.1: No meaningful behavioral validation is visible, or the agent only ran commands that do not exercise the reported scenario; any tests are absent, skipped, unrelated, or merely confirm the code imports/runs.
scale.2: Weak validation exists but is superficial: it checks a narrow implementation detail, printed output, a happy path, aggregate statistics that could be satisfied by wrong fixes, or per-branch counts without verifying which specific values/positions are assigned to each branch, while omitting the core behavior or task-specified boundaries.
scale.3: Validation is comparable to the parent trajectory: some relevant behavior is exercised, but important edge cases, fallback/update semantics, exact assertions, exact output enumeration, or per-branch value/position verification are incomplete or not clearly committed.
scale.4: Strong validation directly covers the reported scenario and at least one important boundary condition, with assertions on observable behavior (including exact output enumeration when the fix changes what is produced and per-branch value/position verification when the fix controls per-branch selection) and evidence that the relevant tests ran.
scale.5: Excellent validation would fail on the original bug and distinguishes the fix from likely wrong implementations; it asserts the exact user contract, includes all task-critical branches, enumerates the exact output set when the fix changes what is produced, verifies per-branch value/position assignments independently when the fix controls per-branch selection (not relying on counts or symmetric cases that can mask reversals), is durable in the patch, and the trajectory shows the targeted tests actually executed.

experiences.title: SymPy assumption fixes need API-path and special-value validation
experiences.description: Retrieve when a SymPy task changes logical relationships among assumptions, especially when the user-facing symptom is an `.is_*` property but the trajectory also investigates `ask(Q.*)` predicates. The rubric must distinguish solutions by their semantic effect on assumption propagation and three-valued behavior, not by surface-level completeness properties shared by all candidate fixes.
experiences.context: Applies in the SymPy codebase when the task is about assumption implication propagation such as parity, integer/rational/algebraic, real/complex, finite/infinite, or similar predicates. It is most relevant after the trajectory has identified that old property accessors (`expr.is_*`) and newer predicate queries (`ask(Q.*)`) may use different inference paths, or after the agent has tried modifying one path without fixing the reproducer. It is especially important when special singleton values such as infinities, complex infinity, or NaN have visible three-valued assumption behavior. Activation evidence that the rubric is at risk of narrowing: all candidate fixes touch both the old and new assumption paths, so a criterion checking only 'both systems modified' assigns the same score to every solution and cannot separate correct from incorrect fixes. Do not apply this as a generic rubric for early repository exploration, for tasks that only touch concrete numeric handlers without symbolic assumption inference, or for non-SymPy projects where there is no visible dual assumptions architecture.
experiences.experience: Prior rubrics in this cluster often asked for understanding SymPy's assumption rule system, correct old-vs-new targeting, consistency between `.is_*` and `ask(Q.*)`, and preservation of special values. That theme is useful, but only if the criterion requires observable implementation and validation evidence. It is too weak to reward merely finding `FactRules`, reading handlers, or stating that there are two systems; several trajectories had that understanding while still making no valid patch, looping on greps/stash checks, or changing only one ineffective path. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent demonstrates that the user-visible accessor is driven by the old assumption closure, that any new predicate facts are kept in sync through the generated-data workflow when touched, and that both APIs are re-run on the reported symbolic case. It should also require explicit safeguards for SymPy's special values: broad rules such as old-style `real -> finite` or `complex -> finite` are tempting because of mathematical documentation, but they can conflict with existing infinity semantics; direct `even/odd/integer -> finite` changes can also have contrapositive effects on non-finite objects, so the trajectory must check whether those changes intentionally preserve or update `None` vs `False` behavior. Prioritize visible evidence such as passing reproducer output for `Symbol(..., even=True).is_finite`, corresponding `ask(Q.finite(...))` behavior, regenerated predicate facts when applicable, targeted tests or sanity checks for infinities/NaN/complex infinity, and absence of unresolved contradictions or repeated non-progress commands. Avoid a criterion that simply says 'modify both assumption systems' without checking whether the semantic implication chosen is safe and validated. When a surface property such as 'both paths modified' or 'both comparison sites guarded' is shared by all candidate fixes, scoring on that property collapses all solutions to a single value and is uninformative. The rubric must instead identify the semantic distinction that actually separates correct from incorrect solutions — the specific implication direction chosen, its effect on three-valued `None` vs `False` behavior for non-finite values, or the control-flow consequence of a guard — and score on that distinction. A close-looking contraindication: a rubric that checks 'both `.is_*` and `ask(Q.*)` are modified' appears to follow the dual-path guidance but is uninformative when every candidate solution modifies both; the distinguishing axis is whether the semantic implication preserves three-valued behavior for special values, not whether both paths were touched. Before generating rubrics, perform a discriminativeness pre-check over the visible continuations: if all continuations inherit the same already-applied assumption fix or repeat materially identical diffs, an implementation-correctness criterion is non-discriminative even if semantically true — exclude it and score instead on continuation-specific validation breadth and final artifact emission. The final completion output should include the submitted patch/diff; a continuation that displayed a diff in an earlier command but whose final completion output lacks the patch text should be capped or lowered because the public final artifact is ambiguous. Do not credit workflow bookkeeping commands such as stash, pop, or patch-file creation/retries unless they produce task-relevant public evidence such as reproducer output, predicate query results, or special-value checks. Abstain from scoring on a shared-property axis when the trajectory does not show enough diff or code detail to determine the semantic effect of the change, or when all candidate solutions genuinely produce the same semantic effect on the reported case and no distinguishing axis exists.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Validated dual-path assumption propagation with semantic-effect scoring
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show a safe, validated assumption-propagation fix for the reported symbolic property accessor, not just conceptual exploration. Strong evidence includes identifying the old `.is_*` assumption closure as necessary for the user-visible symptom, keeping newer `ask(Q.*)` predicate facts consistent if they are modified, regenerating generated predicate data through the documented workflow rather than hand-editing it, and validating both the reported accessor and corresponding predicate query. The trajectory should also account for SymPy's three-valued assumptions on special non-finite values, avoiding broad finite implications that create contradictions or unintentionally collapse `None` into `False` without deliberate test updates. The rubric must score on the semantic effect of the chosen implication — whether it preserves or correctly updates three-valued behavior for non-finite values — not on surface properties shared by all candidate fixes such as 'both assumption systems modified.' Before scoring, perform a discriminativeness pre-check: if all continuations inherit the same already-applied fix, implementation-correctness criteria are non-discriminative and should be excluded. The final completion output should include the submitted patch/diff; a continuation that displayed a diff earlier but whose final completion output lacks the patch text should be capped or lowered. Do not credit workflow bookkeeping commands such as stash, pop, or patch-file creation/retries unless they produce task-relevant public evidence.

required_visible_evidence: recognizes the distinction between old `.is_*` assumptions and newer `ask(Q.*)` predicates
targets the path that actually drives the reported accessor
updates or regenerates new predicate facts if that system is touched
runs the original symbolic reproducer after changes
checks special non-finite values and three-valued assumption behavior
diff or code detail sufficient to determine the semantic effect of the chosen implication on `None` vs `False` for non-finite values
final completion output includes the submitted patch/diff text
unsafe_shortcuts_to_penalize: only editing predicate known facts while `.is_*` remains unchanged
adding broad old-style real/complex-to-finite rules without infinity validation
rewarding repeated searches or conceptual notes without a working validated change
ignoring generated-data workflow after changing new assumption facts
scoring on 'both assumption systems modified' when all candidate fixes share that property — this collapses all solutions to one score and is uninformative
crediting stash/pop/patch-file bookkeeping or path retries without behavior-specific validation evidence
scoring implementation correctness when all continuations inherit the same already-applied fix
close_looking_exclusions: A rubric that checks 'both `.is_*` and `ask(Q.*)` are modified' looks like it follows the dual-path guidance but is uninformative when every candidate solution modifies both paths; the distinguishing axis is the semantic safety of the implication for three-valued special values, not the mere fact of touching both systems

A fix that modifies both paths but uses a broad `real -> finite` implication looks complete but may incorrectly collapse `None` to `False` for infinities — the surface property 'both paths modified' does not distinguish this from a safe targeted fix
Two fixes that both pass the original reproducer may differ in three-valued behavior on edge cases — reproducer output alone is insufficient when all candidates share the same reproducer result

A continuation that displayed a diff in an earlier command but whose final completion output lacks the patch text — the public final artifact is ambiguous and should be capped or lowered even if earlier validation was visible
metadata.abstention_boundary: Abstain from scoring on a shared-property axis when the trajectory does not show enough diff or code detail to determine the semantic effect of the change on three-valued behavior, or when all candidate solutions genuinely produce the same semantic effect on the reported case and no distinguishing axis exists. Also abstain on final-artifact emission when the visible prefix cannot distinguish whether the patch/diff was actually emitted in the final completion output.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of implementing or validating assumption propagation; the trajectory is limited to repository browsing, repeated greps, or an ineffective edit with the original accessor still unresolved.
scale.2: Some relevant investigation of assumption code paths, but the trajectory targets only one API path, makes a risky broad implication, or lacks any post-change reproducer showing the reported `.is_*` behavior fixed.
scale.3: Partial progress comparable to the parent trajectory: the agent understands old vs new assumptions and may fix or inspect one path, but evidence remains incomplete because `ask(Q.*)` consistency, generated facts, or special-value regressions are unresolved. A rubric that scores only on 'both paths modified' — a property shared by all candidates — should not exceed this level because it cannot distinguish correct from incorrect semantic choices.
scale.4: Strong progress: the trajectory targets the correct old assumption mechanism, keeps the new predicate path in mind or updated when needed, reruns the reported symbolic case, and performs at least basic infinity/NaN sanity checks, though some edge-case or test-suite validation may still be incomplete. If the final completion output does not include the submitted patch/diff, cap at this level even if earlier validation was visible.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence of a safe assumption fix: both the reported `.is_*` accessor and corresponding `ask(Q.*)` query behave correctly, generated predicate data is updated through the documented process if applicable, targeted regression tests are added or run, special non-finite values retain deliberate three-valued behavior without contradictions, and the final completion output includes the submitted patch/diff. The rubric distinguishes this level by the semantic safety of the chosen implication and the presence of the final artifact, not merely by the number of paths modified.

experiences.title: Decode byte protocol tokens instead of stringifying their repr
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python 2/3 compatibility bug involves a bytes value that semantically represents text, especially an HTTP method or other protocol token, being converted with `str`/`builtin_str` and then used as if it were decoded text. When the trajectory shows distinct diagnostic or repair competencies—such as reproducing the repr-like token symptom, identifying why the conversion is wrong, locating the conversion path, and placing the decode—maintain separate focused rubrics rather than collapsing them into one broad patch or diagnosis criterion.
experiences.context: Applies in Python libraries or compatibility layers where the task report explicitly shows Python 3 bytes such as `b'GET'` becoming the literal text `"b'GET'"`, and the trajectory has found or is reasoning about the conversion site before request/protocol preparation plus an existing native-string conversion helper or equivalent decode path. It is most useful once the agent has inspected the relevant code path enough to distinguish semantic text bytes from values where string representation is intended. It may be premature during pure codebase exploration, and it should not be applied broadly to every `builtin_str`/`str` usage, such as numeric header values or logging/debug representations where repr-like stringification is acceptable. Separate root-cause and fix-correctness rubrics are warranted when the trajectory contains evidence of both (a) examining why `str`/`builtin_str` produces repr-like output on Python 3 and (b) a diff or concrete plan placing the decode before uppercasing or sending; these are independent because an agent can understand the bytes-text boundary but place the decode incorrectly, or place the decode correctly without articulating why `str(bytes)` is wrong. If reproduction of the symptom or localization of the relevant path varies across trajectories, those may be separate lower-weight positive rubrics, but they must not replace the dedicated root-cause and fix-placement dimensions.
experiences.experience:
The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the actual compatibility contract: byte-string HTTP methods must be decoded to native text before uppercasing or sending, so `b'GET'` becomes `GET`, not `"b'GET'"`, while ordinary string methods keep working. This criterion is discriminative because the visible trajectory often contains decisive evidence: the agent locates the conversion before request creation, confirms that Python 3 maps the compatibility alias to `str`, observes or demonstrates that `str(bytes)` produces a repr-like string, and identifies an existing helper that decodes bytes using the appropriate native-string behavior. A better rubric should judge semantic normalization and preservation of existing string behavior, not merely whether the agent replaced a particular line or searched for all uses of the conversion helper.

Maintain a small portfolio of focused positive rubrics when the visible work separates into multiple competencies. A high-weight root-cause rubric should score only explicit understanding that `str`/`builtin_str` on Python 3 turns bytes into repr-like text and that this causes the observed protocol token failure. A separate high-weight fix-correctness rubric should score whether the decode/native-string conversion is placed before uppercasing, request preparation, or sending, and whether ordinary string inputs remain unchanged. If the trajectory evidence makes them useful, add lower-weight positive rubrics for reproducing or demonstrating the symptom and for locating the relevant conversion path; those dimensions are helpful evidence but are not substitutes for root-cause identification or fix placement. Do not merge reproduction, source browsing, root-cause reasoning, and repair correctness into one broad criterion, because an agent may reproduce `"b'GET'"` without knowing why it happens, browse the right function without articulating the bytes/text mechanism, or apply a plausible decode at the wrong point in the flow.

Judge evidence mapping should keep these dimensions independent. Root-cause identification evidence includes recognizing that the problematic conversion uses `str` or a compatibility alias that is `str` on Python 3, recognizing that applying `str` to bytes produces a repr-like value rather than decoded text, and connecting that conversion to the protocol token becoming repr-like text. Fix-correctness evidence includes targeting the method/request preparation path before uppercasing or sending, using an existing native-string conversion helper or equivalent explicit bytes decode, and preserving normal string method inputs. Reproduction evidence includes a focused demonstration that byte input becomes `"b'GET'"`; it should not by itself raise the root-cause score. Code-localization evidence includes finding the relevant method conversion path; it should not by itself raise the fix-correctness score unless the decode placement is visible or clearly reasoned.

Avoid the tempting wrong criterion of requiring all `builtin_str` uses to be changed; other occurrences may intentionally stringify integers or other non-text values. Also avoid over-penalizing inability to run broad validation when the visible failure is an unrelated environment compatibility issue and the agent has validated or reasoned about the conversion logic in a focused way. Do not conflate validation presence with fix correctness; a patch can include test reasoning yet place the decode at the wrong point in the flow. Do not infer root-cause understanding from diff size or patch presence alone. A close-looking case is a patch that adds `.decode()` at the right location but the agent never articulates why `str(bytes)` is wrong on Python 3: this scores high on fix correctness but not on root-cause identification. Conversely, an agent that explains the bytes-text boundary but places the decode after uppercasing should score high on root cause but low on fix correctness.

Abstention boundary: When the trajectory prefix does not show whether the agent examined the conversion semantics or merely patched the line, preserve uncertainty about root-cause understanding rather than inferring it from patch presence. When the diff or plan is not visible enough to show where the decode is placed relative to uppercasing, request preparation, or sending, preserve uncertainty about fix correctness rather than defaulting to a scope-based proxy. When the visible prefix is still in setup or broad exploration before diagnostic reasoning is articulated, do not infer future root-cause identification; score only the evidence that is observable, and keep uncertainty in one dimension from contaminating the others.

experiences.title: Branch-Sensitive Fix Review
experiences.description: Retrieve when the candidate fix changes a conditional, version gate, feature flag, empty/non-empty case split, exception handler path, fallback or legacy branch, or a shared function/helper called from multiple semantic contexts, and correctness depends on preserving all intended behaviors across the affected paths. During optional second-pass rubric-portfolio review, also retrieve when visible task evidence establishes that an existing fallback or legacy branch is itself the buggy behavior; in that case, rubric language must not give positive credit for preserving or recreating that fallback as though it were the unaffected path.
experiences.context: Applies in repair trajectories for Python, Go, or similar codebases at the implementation or final-review stage, after the agent has identified or edited a concrete decision point, fallback path, exception path, or shared helper. It is most useful when the task statement contrasts semantic branches such as flag enabled vs disabled, old vs new backend version, explicit vs implicit value, empty vs non-empty input, normal vs exception path, canonical value vs synthesized fallback, or when a shared function is called from multiple sites with different expectations. Do not retrieve it as the main rubric during early exploration before a concrete branch or call-site has been selected, for purely unconditional refactors, when the modified function is used in only one semantic context, or when the change is purely additive without altering existing behavior. Also abstain when visible evidence shows the conditional or fallback is only a small part of a broader contract such as response formatting, schema migration, or end-to-end error propagation. For fallback-polarity correction, activate only when the public task and visible candidate/rubric text establish that the fallback or legacy branch is the behavior being removed or replaced; do not apply this correction when another public contract explicitly requires that fallback.
experiences.experience:
The original branch-sensitive lesson is to judge whether the fix was checked on both sides of the affected decision point rather than only on the originally failing path. This remains discriminative when a patch adds a separator only for non-empty values, changes behavior behind a version gate or feature flag, adjusts exception handling while preserving the normal path, or modifies a shared helper used by callers with different semantic expectations. Strong evidence identifies the exact predicate, exception handler, fallback branch, or shared function; enumerates the semantic cases or call-site contexts it separates; and uses tests or precise static reasoning to show that the newly fixed path works while intended legacy/default/opposite/other-call-site behavior remains correct.

Small reusable refinement: branch preservation must follow the public contract, not the old code shape. A recurring rubric error is to treat an old synthesized fallback, recomputed default, or legacy branch as something to preserve even when the issue statement identifies that behavior as the bug. If visible evidence says the correct behavior is to use a real propagated value, canonical source, explicit input, or no value rather than inventing a fallback, then any positive rubric, scale level, judge focus, validation example, or failure description that gives medium/high credit for keeping or recreating the old fallback should be deleted or inverted before scoring. Merely lowering its weight is insufficient because the rubric still encodes the wrong implementation contract.

Visible evidence that should trigger this polarity correction includes: the task says a value is already supplied upstream but the failing method recomputes it; labels, identifiers, paths, keys, or outputs are expected to match a rendered or stored canonical value but instead come from name/index/string concatenation or another synthetic source; the candidate rubric praises preserving a fallback for absent data even though the issue says that fallback should no longer be produced; or scale language treats the old branch as a valid partial solution. The dominant implementation criterion should instead ask whether the fix returns, propagates, delegates to, or otherwise derives from the contractually correct source. Equivalent valid implementations should be preserved: the fix may remove the branch, guard it, delegate to a helper, change the caller, or return an explicit no-value result, so long as the visible behavior matches the public contract. Do not penalize a value merely because its string shape resembles the old synthetic fallback; penalize only when the implementation or rubric gives credit for sourcing it from the disallowed recomputation or fallback.

Keep validation proportional. A small regression criterion may check that truly unaffected branches, public boundaries, or existing callers still behave correctly, but do not let broad architecture coverage or validation breadth displace the primary polarity of the changed branch. Do not substitute a single reproducer, an if-statement, file location, root-cause-vs-caller placement, or the number of call sites mentioned for concrete behavioral evidence. Prefer paired examples, branch matrices, call-site enumeration with context-specific reasoning, and tests or inspection showing: the originally broken path no longer fails; the existing relevant behavior that remains part of the public contract is preserved; and any old fallback identified as buggy is not treated as a correct partial implementation.

Abstain from this card when no concrete branch, fallback, exception path, or shared helper is visible; when the public contract explicitly requires preserving the fallback under some condition; when the portfolio already treats the disallowed fallback as a low-score or failure case and the highest-weight implementation rubric states the correct source of truth; or when the main task is a broader non-branch contract better handled by a more specific rubric.

experiences.title: PostgreSQL dbshell psql argument-order invariant
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django-style database shell task concerns PostgreSQL `psql` ignoring extra `dbshell` parameters because they are placed after the database name.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django repository where the task explicitly states that PostgreSQL `psql` requires command-line options or user-provided dbshell parameters before the positional database name. The trajectory should have reached the PostgreSQL dbshell/client argument construction code, or at least identified that backend-specific command construction is the likely repair site. This guidance is strongest once the agent has inspected or edited the argument list builder and there is visible evidence about where `parameters` and the database name are appended. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before PostgreSQL-specific code is found, and should not be generalized to other database backends whose CLIs may intentionally order database names and parameters differently.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic command-line contract: for PostgreSQL, generated `psql` arguments must keep the executable and connection flags first, then append user-supplied dbshell parameters, and leave the database name as the final positional argument when present. This was discriminative because the task is not about generic dbshell execution, subprocess handling, or installing/running tests; it is about one ordering invariant that determines whether `psql -c ... dbname` works instead of treating `-c` as an ignored extra argument. A better rubric should judge visible evidence that the agent located the PostgreSQL-specific command builder, recognized the existing `dbname`-before-`parameters` bug, changed only the ordering so parameters precede the database name, and preserved existing user/host/port/password/SSL/environment behavior. Manual or unit-test evidence should be valued when it directly prints or asserts the constructed argument list with parameters before the database name. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as requiring successful full test-suite execution in an environment with missing dependencies, rewarding only test updates, changing shared dbshell/base client behavior, or applying PostgreSQL ordering rules to MySQL/SQLite/Oracle clients. When the implementation contract requires setting subprocess environment variables (e.g., PGSSLMODE/PGSSLROOTCERT/PGSSLCERT/PGSSLKEY for SSL options), do not add a secondary rubric about environment isolation or minimal environment footprint—such a rubric anti-correlates with the correct approach and can invert the ranking by rewarding implementations that avoid environment variables. Preserving EXISTING environment behavior (e.g., not breaking PGPASSWORD handling or SIGINT handling) is part of the implementation contract and belongs in the primary rubric; penalizing ADDING new environment variables is the specific error to avoid. A single rubric focused on the exact implementation contract is preferable to multiple rubrics where a secondary quality concern displaces the primary distinction. If the visible trajectory prefix is truncated and does not reveal whether the implementation uses environment variables or command-line flags for SSL options, preserve uncertainty about the delivery mechanism rather than assuming either approach or scoring based on secondary quality proxies.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserve PostgreSQL psql argument ordering contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the trajectory is converging on the PostgreSQL `psql` argument-order fix: user-provided dbshell parameters/options must be inserted before the optional database name, with the database name remaining the final positional argument, while existing connection flags and environment handling remain unchanged. When the contract requires setting subprocess environment variables (e.g., PGSSL* for SSL options), adding those variables is correct behavior, not a violation of environment preservation.

required_visible_evidence: Identifies PostgreSQL-specific dbshell/client command construction as the relevant implementation area
Recognizes that placing the database name before additional parameters causes `psql` to ignore later options
Shows or describes an edit that appends user parameters before appending the database name
Preserves existing executable, user, host, port, password, SSL, and environment option behavior (i.e., does not break existing PGPASSWORD handling, SIGINT handling, or connection flag construction)
When SSL options are present, maps them to PGSSL* subprocess environment variables rather than invalid psql command-line flags such as --ssl-mode or --ssl-cert
Optionally validates with an argument-list assertion or printout demonstrating parameters before database name
non_requirements: Full test-suite success is not required when dependency or settings setup blocks execution
Other database backends need not be changed
Regression tests are helpful but should not substitute for the implementation ordering fix

A secondary rubric about environment isolation or minimal environment footprint must not be added when the contract requires setting subprocess environment variables; such a rubric anti-correlates with correctness and can invert the ranking by rewarding implementations that avoid environment variables
When the visible trajectory prefix is truncated and does not reveal the SSL delivery mechanism, preserve uncertainty rather than scoring based on secondary quality proxies

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has found the PostgreSQL command builder or understood the `psql` ordering requirement.
scale.2: The agent mentions PostgreSQL or dbshell parameters, but the visible plan or edits do not clearly ensure parameters appear before the database name.
scale.3: The agent has identified the correct ordering issue and likely target area, but the visible evidence is incomplete, unverified, or risks disturbing unrelated connection behavior.
scale.4: The agent visibly changes or plans the correct localized ordering so parameters precede the database name, with reasonable preservation of existing connection options and correct use of subprocess environment variables where the contract requires them.
scale.5: The agent makes the localized PostgreSQL ordering fix, preserves surrounding connection/environment semantics (including correct PGSSL* variable handling when SSL options are present), and provides direct validation or test expectations showing generated `psql` args with parameters before the final database name.

experiences.title: Contract-Level Behavioral Test Evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an agent claims validation through added tests, changed expected outputs, or ad hoc scripts for a behavior-specific bug or feature; judge whether those tests assert the actual user-visible contract — including the exact set of produced values when the fix changes what is yielded or returned — rather than merely exercising code paths or confirming aggregate statistics match. When the validation footprint includes a newly created feature-named test module in the project test tree, also judge test-artifact integrity as a distinct evidence axis: the artifact should be intentional, consistent with the intended test contract, and not a conflicting replacement or discovery-breaking file. Do not penalize legitimate new tests merely for being new or temporarily visible outside the final diff; activate this concern only when placement or content visibly conflicts with the intended test contract.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent trajectories across Python, Go, and TypeScript projects after the agent has identified a fix and is using tests or manual scripts as confidence evidence. It is most relevant for tasks involving parsing metadata, fallback ordering, event-driven UI updates, set/membership semantics, deterministic selection, API parameter precedence, or yield/return logic where a patch can look plausible while missing a boundary condition. It also applies when visible changed-file or untracked-file evidence shows a new test module under the project test tree named for the feature being implemented, because such a file can affect whether the validation artifact itself respects the expected test contract. It is less decisive during early exploration, when no implementation exists yet, or for very small localized source fixes whose correctness is directly visible from the changed line and no durable test has been added. Do not retrieve it merely because no formal test was run; absence of tests alone is not a reliable flaw for simple one-line compatibility fixes. Do retrieve it when tests are present but may be superficial, omitted from the submitted diff, only check that code runs, update expectations to match an incorrect intermediate representation, rely on aggregate statistics that can be satisfied by wrong fixes which skip or duplicate items, or introduce a visibly conflicting feature-named test module. Abstain from the aggregate-statistics criterion when the fix does not modify what is produced, or when the exact output cannot be observed from the visible prefix and only aggregate statistics are available. Abstain from the new-test-module integrity criterion when no file listing is visible, the agent only edits an existing test file, the script is clearly outside the project test tree, or the new test file’s placement and content are not visibly in conflict.
experiences.experience:
The prior rubric judged whether validation was meaningful. It was useful when visible test activity revealed whether the agent understood the behavioral contract: strong evidence came from tests that exercised the exact reported scenario, asserted the final observable result, and included important branches such as missing data, fallback paths, resize/update events, explicit override versus default behavior, deterministic ordering, or membership semantics. It correctly flagged trajectories where the agent relied on smoke scripts, repeated commands, changed expected values without checking the real semantic object, or added tests that did not cover the required fallback or edge case. However, it can be misleading if used as a blanket requirement: a tiny, obvious formatting or parameter-default fix may be correct even with weak or no committed tests. A better retrieved rubric should focus on the quality, relevance, and integrity of validation evidence, not on the mere presence, count, or passing status of tests.

Preserve two distinct evidence axes. First, contract validation: tests or scripts should reproduce the reported behavior, assert the user-facing contract exactly, cover task-named boundaries, and be reproducible from the visible trajectory. When a fix modifies what is produced — yielded, returned, emitted, rendered, or copied — matching aggregate statistics such as counts can be a false proxy. The discriminating evidence is whether each expected item appears exactly once with its correct final value. Prefer evidence that enumerates the exact output set over evidence that only checks command success or aggregate counts.

Second, test-artifact integrity: when the validation footprint visibly creates a brand-new feature-named test module under the project test tree, generated rubrics should include a separate positive criterion, or a separately gated subcriterion, that inspects whether the file is a valid intended test artifact. This criterion should distinguish a new feature-named module from edits to an existing test file and from scratch scripts outside the test tree. It should withhold full validation credit from a semantically correct source change if the new test file is visibly a replacement artifact, duplicates or collides with an expected test-module name, has content inconsistent with the requested behavior, changes discovery behavior, contains malformed scaffolding/imports, or otherwise conflicts with the project’s test contract. Conversely, do not lower the score merely because a legitimate test is new or temporarily listed as untracked; there must be visible conflict or unverifiable inconsistency in placement or content.

When generating rubrics from this card, keep polarity positive: award credit for meaningful contract validation and clean test-artifact integrity. Weight validation lower than the core source-behavior criterion when source semantics are also being judged, but make the integrity weight nonzero and decisive enough that a correct source implementation paired with a visibly conflicting new feature-named test module cannot receive the same maximum score as a clean equivalent. A practical mapping is to give the integrity axis a modest separate weight, or require a clean or verified test footprint for the top validation level while allowing uncertainty when file content is not visible. Do not let a test-file concern outrank a clearly incorrect implementation; it is a full-credit gate among otherwise comparable source fixes, not a substitute for behavioral correctness.

Prioritize evidence that tests would fail on the original bug, assert exact semantic outputs or state changes, include boundary branches named by the task, enumerate exact produced items when relevant, and are included as durable artifacts when appropriate. For new feature-named test modules, prioritize visible file-list evidence, path placement under the test tree, whether the file is newly created versus an edit, whether its assertions match the intended contract, and whether its imports/naming support normal discovery. Deprioritize broad suite pass status without relevant assertions, superficial print scripts, aggregate counts where exact outputs matter, updated expectations that mirror an intermediate implementation, and any rubric that grants full credit solely from correct source logic while ignoring a visibly conflicting validation artifact. Preserve equivalent implementations and uncertainty: score the observable behavior and artifact integrity, not exact wording, file naming style, or test count.

experiences.title: Centralized Expression Type-Inference Alignment
experiences.description: Use when an expression-system task concerns result-type or output-field inference, or dispatch from a generic expression/operator node to a more specialized semantic node, and the visible design relies on a centralized type-resolution registry, type-combination table, or resolver/dispatch path. In optional second-pass rubric refinement, ensure the highest-weight criterion is the precise resolved type-flow or conversion contract, not test execution volume or duplicated regression concerns.
experiences.context: Applies after visible evidence shows that expression construction succeeds but result-type inference, output-field resolution, or generic-to-specialized expression dispatch is failing. Strong activation evidence includes inspection or modification of a centralized connector/type/result matrix, resolver method, dispatch table, or comparable type-flow mechanism; comparison with analogous supported operator/type combinations; or before/after checks showing that resolved operand types determine whether a result type or specialized expression node should be selected. It is less useful before the layer of failure is identified. Do not apply to backend-specific SQL behavior, parser/operator construction problems, unrelated runtime math functions, caller-side explicit output-field or wrapper workarounds when those are the intended solution, or tasks without a centralized type-resolution/expression-dispatch mechanism. Abstain if the rubric portfolio already has a single highest-weight implementation-contract rubric separated from validation, no duplicate edge/regression double-counting, and no evidence of a resolver/type-flow weighting error.
experiences.experience:
The reusable semantic lesson is to center rubrics on the exact type-flow contract: once child operands or subexpressions have been resolved, the implementation should use the resolved output types and the relevant connector/operator/context to select the correct result type or specialized semantic expression, without changing unrelated expression semantics. For registry-based designs, this often means aligning the missing operator or type combination with the existing centralized rules rather than adding broad scattered special cases. For resolver/dispatch designs, it means converting the already-resolved generic expression to the intended specialized node only under the precise supported type conditions.

Before scoring, correct a recurring rubric error: do not let test execution, broad regression penalties, or multiple overlapping edge-case rubrics outweigh the primary implementation contract. The highest-weight non-style rubric should reward the precise resolved-expression contract and should usually carry the largest share of non-style weight. It should explicitly preserve equivalent valid implementations: a clean registry entry, a focused resolver branch, an idempotent specialized-node resolver, a guard against re-conversion, or a direct return/construction of the specialized node can all be valid if they use resolved operand types, satisfy the same semantic boundary, and do not create an infinite resolution path. Do not mark a direct return of a replacement semantic node as lacking recursion handling merely because it lacks a separate guard; penalize recursion only when the visible patch actually re-resolves the newly constructed node or otherwise creates an infinite or repeated conversion path.

Keep the portfolio compact and non-overlapping. Prefer: one primary implementation-contract rubric; one lower-weight edge/regression-preservation rubric covering adjacent valid combinations, unsupported combinations that must remain unsupported, and existing expression paths that should remain unchanged; a small locality/code-quality rubric if useful; and optionally a low-weight validation rubric. Split validation from correctness: targeted tests, scripts, or framework test attempts are useful evidence, but local setup failures, missing tools, settings/import issues, or unrelated configuration errors should not reduce the implementation-contract score. If a negative regression rubric remains, cap it below the primary contract and make it evidence-gated: apply it only for concrete visible behavior caused by the change, such as wrong resolved type, over-broadened supported combinations, malformed registry/resolver logic, wrong specialized operation, or a previously valid expression path now failing. Remove negative rubrics that duplicate the same failures already covered by a positive edge-preservation rubric at comparable weight.

experiences.title: Contract-Level Behavioral Test Evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an agent claims validation through added tests, changed expected outputs, manual checks, or ad hoc scripts for a behavior-specific bug or feature; judge whether that evidence asserts the actual user-visible contract rather than merely exercising code paths, confirming command success, matching aggregate statistics, or relying on cosmetic diff exactness. When direct behavioral validation is visibly blocked by environment or dependency errors, a low-weight rubric may credit post-edit confirmation of the final semantic source state, but it must not replace the primary correctness rubric.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent trajectories after the agent has identified or implemented a fix and is using tests, scripts, manual commands, or file inspection as confidence evidence. It is most relevant for tasks involving parsing metadata, fallback ordering, event-driven updates, set or membership semantics, deterministic selection, API parameter precedence, argument/type contracts, or yield/return/output logic where a patch can look plausible while missing a boundary condition. Do not retrieve it merely because no formal test was run; absence of tests alone is not a reliable flaw for simple localized fixes whose correctness is directly inspectable. Do retrieve it when validation is present but may be superficial, skipped, omitted from the final patch, only checks that code runs, updates expectations to match an implementation artifact, relies on aggregate statistics that can be satisfied by skipped or duplicated outputs, or when a direct runtime check was attempted but visibly failed for environmental reasons unrelated to the semantic fix. Abstain from the aggregate-output criterion when the fix does not modify what is yielded, returned, emitted, or otherwise produced, or when the exact output set is not observable from the visible trajectory.
experiences.experience:
Use this card to refine rubric portfolios toward contract-level evidence. Strong validation evidence reproduces the reported scenario, asserts the final observable behavior, covers task-named boundaries such as missing data, fallback paths, update events, explicit override versus default behavior, deterministic ordering, or membership semantics, and would fail on the original bug. Weak evidence merely shows that commands ran, broad suites passed, printed values looked plausible, or aggregate counts matched. Avoid the blanket mistakes 'tests pass, therefore the patch is good' and 'no tests, therefore the patch is bad.'

When a fix changes what is produced, aggregate statistics are a common false proxy. A wrong implementation can skip, duplicate, or omit items while still reporting the same number of processed files, returned rows, copied entries, or emitted events. In those cases, prefer validation that enumerates the exact output set: each expected item appears exactly once with the correct final value.

Additional reusable correction for blocked runtime validation: if the primary correctness rubric already captures the semantic implementation contract, but its highest level depends on a direct runtime/manual behavioral check that visibly cannot run because of an import, dependency, setup, or environment error, do not force all otherwise correct localized edits below stronger-but-unavailable runtime evidence. Instead, if differentiation is needed, add at most one low-weight positive criterion for post-edit final-state confirmation. This criterion should reward visible evidence that, after making the edit, the agent rereads or otherwise displays the modified region and the output confirms the intended semantic change while preserving necessary surrounding behavior. A successful shell edit command alone is weaker than post-edit readback, because it does not prove the final file state. This criterion should remain subordinate to the primary implementation-contract rubric and should not let an incorrect or unedited solution outrank a semantically correct one.

Prohibited recurring rubric error: do not rank semantically equivalent implementations by patch character count, trailing whitespace, line length, exact diff shape, or other non-semantic cosmetic metrics. Cosmetic exactness is not behavioral validation unless the visible task contract is itself about formatting or whitespace-sensitive output. Visible evidence that activates this correction includes: a direct behavioral validation attempt fails for an environmental reason; the intended fix is a small localized semantic change whose final source state can be inspected; and candidate trajectories differ mainly in whether they confirmed the edited file after the edit, not in the meaning of the implementation. Preserve equivalent valid implementations: different edit commands, formatting choices, or refactor-neutral spellings should receive the same primary correctness score when they implement the same contract.

Abstain from adding the post-edit confirmation sub-criterion when runtime validation succeeds and directly distinguishes the work, when visible final diffs show a real semantic difference that the primary correctness rubric should score, when all relevant trajectories have the same final-state confirmation status, when the task requires broad multi-file integration evidence rather than a localized source-state check, or when the only available evidence is aggregate statistics for behavior whose exact output cannot be observed.

experiences.title: End-to-End Protobuf Option Follow-Through
experiences.description: Use when a Go/gRPC service task adds a new request option that changes server behavior, especially when the trajectory has edited the .proto file or generated code and is trying to honor the option in request handling.
experiences.context: Applies in Go projects with checked-in protobuf/gRPC/gateway/OpenAPI outputs where the requested fix introduces a new boolean request field that controls conditional error handling in a batch/server path. It is most useful after the agent has identified the protobuf request message and the server loop, or after it has attempted generation/manual generated-file edits. It is less useful for purely internal behavior changes with no API schema evolution, for repositories that do not check in generated protobuf artifacts, or very early exploration before the agent has found whether the API contract is protobuf-backed. If generation tooling is unavailable and the agent hand-edits generated files, this criterion becomes more important, not less, because hand-added struct fields/getters may compile while protobuf reflection, JSON/gateway, and documentation remain inconsistent.
experiences.experience:
The recurring useful judgment is that adding the visible option name to the source proto or manually adding a Go struct field is not enough. A strong rubric for these trajectories should evaluate end-to-end follow-through: the API schema must expose the new field with a backward-compatible default, generated artifacts must be regenerated or consistently updated, server-side batch logic must use the new field to skip only typed not-found errors while preserving existing fail-fast behavior when false, and tests must cover both enabled and disabled behavior. Previous narrow rubrics that focused only on the batch loop were useful when the trajectory had not yet touched core logic, but they became too lenient once the agent added plausible server code while leaving generated protobuf/gateway/swagger state incomplete or unverified. Conversely, a rubric focused only on protobuf regeneration can miss an implementation that exposes the field but never honors it. Avoid tempting proxies such as: the proto contains `exclude_not_found`; a getter exists in generated Go; `go build` or an existing batch test passes; or the agent tried `make proto` but failed due missing tooling. Prioritize visible evidence of a clean generated-code path or comprehensive equivalent updates, typed not-found discrimination rather than string/new-error comparison or swallowing all errors, unchanged default behavior for omitted/false options, preservation of existing response request ID and timing behavior, and new regression tests for mixed existing/missing requests.

A decisive observable distinction: visible test failure output (FAILED, Error, Traceback) in the trajectory indicates the implementation is broken, even if some tests show success or the agent claims tests pass. Do not conflate 'a test was executed' with 'a test passed.' A rubric that scores a trajectory high because tests were run—while ignoring visible failure output—produces severe anti-correlation: broken implementations with visible failures can score as high as correct ones. When the trajectory shows test execution results, inspect them for pass/fail status; visible failure output is a strong negative signal that must suppress the score on any correctness criterion regardless of how many other proxy signals look positive. Similarly, edge-case or secondary criteria (e.g., a specific error-type sub-case, a particular gateway field naming variant) must not dominate the portfolio at the expense of the core implementation-contract rubric; the core contract criterion must carry weight at least equal to the highest edge-case criterion. A portfolio narrowed to a single edge-case rubric while omitting or under-weighting the core contract causes correct trajectories to be penalized and broken ones to be rewarded.

When the task requires a code change to produce specific server behavior, the rubric portfolio must include at least one implementation-contract rubric evaluating whether the code change produces the correct end-to-end behavior, and this rubric should carry the highest weight. Validation or environment rubrics (build tooling availability, test runner setup, dependency installation, installed-package testing) should be secondary or excluded when the core task is a code behavior change. Narrowing the portfolio to a single validation-targeting rubric while dropping all implementation-contract rubrics causes severe anti-correlation: correct trajectories that modified the target file and demonstrated correct behavior get penalized for the validation proxy, while trajectories with no code changes receive the best scores. Concrete activation evidence: the trajectory shows the agent editing source files (proto, generated Go, server handler), running tests, or demonstrating output behavior, and the task requires a code change to produce specific server behavior. Specific behavior boundary: a trajectory with a non-empty diff in the target source files that demonstrates correct behavior should score higher than a trajectory with an empty diff, regardless of validation proxy signals; using an installed package version for testing is not a negative signal if the target source file was also modified with the correct change. Close-looking contraindication: a trajectory that has a non-empty diff in the proto file and generated code but does not honor the option in server logic may appear to have made progress but still produces incorrect behavior; a trajectory with a large diff that produces runtime errors should not score higher than a trajectory with a small diff that produces correct behavior. A trajectory with visible test failure output (FAILED, Error, Traceback) must not score high on any correctness criterion, even if other tests pass or the agent reports success. Abstain when the visible prefix shows no behavior demonstration and the diff alone cannot distinguish correct from incorrect behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete API Option Contract and Semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a complete implementation of a new protobuf-backed batch request option: the source request schema adds a backward-compatible boolean field; generated API artifacts are regenerated or consistently updated without corrupt manual edits; the server batch loop reads the generated option and, only when true, skips individual requests that fail with the project's typed not-found error while returning all other errors and preserving the default fail-fast behavior when false; existing response identifier and timing behavior remains intact; and regression tests or a clear test plan cover mixed existing/missing requests with the option enabled, missing requests with it disabled, and non-not-found errors. This rubric should carry the highest weight in the portfolio; validation or environment rubrics should be secondary or excluded when the core task is a code behavior change. Edge-case criteria must not exceed the weight of this core contract criterion.

metadata.environment: Go service using protobuf/gRPC with checked-in generated request types and gateway/documentation artifacts
required_visible_evidence: protobuf request message contains a new optional/default-false boolean field with a fresh tag and appropriate JSON/Go naming
generated code or equivalent artifacts are updated consistently, not merely a hand-added field/getter with stale descriptors or gateway/docs
batch request handler reads the generated option field
not-found detection uses the repository's typed error mechanism, such as errors.As or an established helper, rather than comparing to a newly constructed error or matching strings
when the option is false or omitted, the first not-found error still fails the batch
when the option is true, only not-found subrequests are omitted and successful responses retain existing request identifier and timing conventions
tests or planned tests exercise enabled partial success, disabled fail-fast behavior, and non-not-found error propagation
visible test execution results show PASS or SUCCESS status for relevant tests, not merely that tests were executed
common_negative_cues: protoc or generation failed and the trajectory proceeds with partial manual generated-file edits
only the .proto file or Go struct/getter is changed
generated descriptor, gateway, or documentation consistency is not considered in a repository that checks those in
server logic skips all errors or uses brittle error equality/string checks
portfolio narrowed to a single validation-targeting rubric while dropping all implementation-contract rubrics
visible test failure output (FAILED, Error, Traceback) in the trajectory is ignored while test execution is treated as passage
edge-case criteria dominate the portfolio while the core implementation-contract rubric is under-weighted or omitted

scale.1: No meaningful end-to-end progress: the option is absent from the API contract or the trajectory is still only exploring without a concrete schema and server plan.
scale.2: Weak progress: the source schema or generated struct is partially edited, but generated artifacts are incomplete/unverified or server behavior is not implemented.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the option is exposed and some batch-loop logic exists, but there are gaps such as stale generated metadata, no gateway/documentation consistency, weak error typing, or missing tests.
scale.4: Strong progress: schema, generated types, and server semantics are mostly correct, with typed not-found handling and default fail-fast behavior preserved, but validation or one generated/test surface remains incomplete.
scale.5: Strongest progress: the trajectory shows a coherent generated API update, correct conditional server semantics for only not-found subrequests, preserved identifiers/timing, and targeted regression coverage for enabled, disabled, and non-not-found cases with visible passing test results.

experiences.title: Minimal Serialization Hook for Autocomplete Results
experiences.description: Use this when a Django admin autocomplete task asks for a low-risk refactor that exposes per-result JSON serialization as an overridable hook while preserving the existing response contract. The central contract is the admin autocomplete result serialization/display path, not model fields, storage schema, migrations, or broad validation behavior.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source-tree trajectory where the task specifically requests refactoring an admin autocomplete JSON view so subclasses can add extra fields without overriding the full request-handling method. It is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence from an implementation summary, inspected diff, source output, or direct behavior check showing changes to the autocomplete view class and its result serialization path. The criterion is less useful during very early exploration before any implementation exists, and it should not be replaced by a test-only criterion unless the task instructions explicitly require new regression tests. It may also be irrelevant for broader autocomplete behavior changes involving permissions, query construction, widget wiring, or response schema redesign rather than extracting the existing per-object result mapping.
experiences.experience:
For this task family, the most predictive rubric focuses on the exact extension-point refactor: the view should gain an overridable per-object serialization method, and the existing response-building method should call that hook for each object in the results list. This is useful because the requested change is intentionally small: preserving all request processing, permission checks, queryset/context construction, pagination, and the default Select2-compatible JSON shape matters more than adding unrelated behavior.

Strong positive evidence is visible source, diff, or direct behavior output showing that the admin autocomplete response construction delegates each result object to a hook with the needed object and target-field information, and that the default hook preserves the original item mapping, especially string conversion for `id` and `text`. Equivalent implementations are acceptable: the hook name need not be identical if it is clearly overridable, receives enough information to serialize the object for the target field, is invoked for every returned result, and keeps the existing top-level response and pagination semantics unchanged.

When generating or applying rubrics, make this admin serialization hook the high-weight positive implementation criterion. Full credit should require both sides of the contract: an actual per-result hook and unchanged default autocomplete response behavior. Supporting validation, such as a subclass override that adds an extra field or existing admin autocomplete checks passing, can strengthen confidence but should not become the main requirement when the implementation evidence is decisive.

Do not displace the implementation contract with unrelated completeness requirements. Model field edits, migrations, schema changes, database serialization changes, form-field validation changes, broad JSON validation, or generalized test-running are not mandatory for a task whose visible issue is how admin autocomplete results are serialized or displayed. Such work is neutral unless it visibly breaks the autocomplete contract; it cannot compensate for a missing hook, a hook that is not used to build each result, a changed identifier/display label mapping, or altered permission/query/pagination flow.

Evidence gating matters. Only distinguish continuations when the paused view exposes the relevant changed lines, source output, implementation summary with enough specificity, or a direct behavior check of the autocomplete serialization path. If the view only shows broad exploration, changed-file counts, generic command attempts, dependency or test setup issues, or summaries that do not reveal whether the hook exists and is called, preserve uncertainty with neutral or tied scores rather than inferring correctness from proxies.

experiences.title: Preserve equivalent implementations while discriminating rubrics by materially different correctness dimensions
